FAQ: Chery Tiggo 8 Export from China

How much does it cost to import a Chery Tiggo 8 Pro to Russia in 2026?

On a broker-cleared example with a $15,600 CIF value at Vladivostok, the total import burden runs $16,200–19,600: customs duty of $5,900–6,300, 20% VAT of $4,300–4,500, a utilization fee of $5,200–7,800 depending on the current coefficient, excise of about $110–125, and $700–900 in broker and documentation fees. That puts the cleared vehicle at roughly $31,800–35,200 on the ground. Coefficients change by federal decree, so confirm with your clearing broker at order time.

What is the Tiggo 8 Pro FOB price at Nansha Port?

Indicative September 2026 FOB Nansha pricing runs from $14,200 for the 1.6T Comfort 5-seat to $15,600 for the 1.6T Luxury 7-seat, with the Tiggo 8 Pro Max 2.0T at about $17,800. The Tiggo 9 starts near $22,500 in 2WD 8AT form and $24,800 for the AWD Flagship. Final quotes depend on trim, color and dealer-stock allocation at the time of deposit.

Vladivostok or Novorossiysk — which Russian port should I choose?

For Far East, Siberian and Ural buyers, Vladivostok: $1,800–2,400 per vehicle by RoRo, 5–8 days at sea, customs release in 4–8 working days, then TransSib rail to Moscow in 8–14 days. For European Russia, Novorossiysk via Suez costs $3,800–5,200 and takes 28–35 days — choose it only when the final destination sits west of the Volga and the buyer can absorb the longer transit.

What documents does a Chinese Chery SUV need at Russian customs?

Four items drive the file: the commercial invoice and bill of lading from the exporter, a documentary EAC declaration (the Tiggo 8 Pro is type-approved, so no physical testing), the SBKTS certificate of vehicle safety construction, and the EPTS electronic passport. Your clearing broker prepares the SBKTS and EPTS from our export documents; budget $700–900 for the service bundle.

Uzbekistan, outside the EAEU, has been cutting passenger-vehicle duties since 2023 and clears directly through Tashkent brokers. Each route needs its own broker-side cost sheet before contracting.

Does the Tiggo 8 Pro come with 7 seats and Russian-language multimedia?

Both seat layouts exist: the Comfort trim ships as a 5-seater, while Luxury and Pro Max trims offer the 5- or 7-seat configuration. The Chinese-spec head unit is Mandarin-first and needs a region flash for full Russian language, costing $280–420 in Moscow — we confirm the flash decision with you before the deposit so it is a planned line item, not a post-sale dispute.

content:
Why TPMS Is the Fastest-Growing Replacement Part Category

Tire pressure monitoring sensors stopped being optional hardware a decade ago. The United States mandated TPMS on all light vehicles from 2007, the European Union followed in 2014, and China's GB 26149 standard made the system compulsory on every new passenger car from January 2020. That single regulatory wave created a replacement fleet measured in hundreds of millions of vehicles — and every one of those sensors carries an internal battery with a service life of 5 to 10 years.

The arithmetic is what makes TPMS attractive for wholesale distributors. A sedan sold in 2018 is now entering its second or third sensor replacement cycle. A four-sensor set at $6.00 FOB represents $24 of goods that retails for $120-200 fitted in most markets, and the part is small enough that a single carton can hold several hundred units. For repair shops, TPMS service has become a standard upsell attached to every tire replacement and seasonal wheel change.

Kingmay's Guangzhou inventory covers the three platforms that dominate export-destination fleets: Toyota Corolla / Camry / RAV4, Nissan Sentra / Sylphy / X-Trail / Qashqai, and Hyundai Elantra / Tucson / Sonata / Kia Sportage / K5. All sensors are packaged with valve stems, seals and nuts where applicable, labeled with OE-grade references, and available from 50-piece trial orders up to full mixed-container loads.

Direct vs Indirect TPMS: What Distributors Should Stock

Not every tire pressure system uses a physical sensor in the wheel. Understanding the split matters because it determines which part numbers actually move in your market.

System type How it works Typical vehicles Parts sold
Direct TPMSPressure sensor inside each wheel transmits by RF to the body control moduleMost US-spec vehicles, all post-2020 Chinese-market cars, most Korean and Japanese models for GCC and Latin AmericaSensor units, valve stems, service kits
Indirect TPMS (iTPMS)Uses ABS wheel-speed data to infer pressure loss; no sensor in the wheelMany European-market Hyundai and Kia models, some budget trimsNo dedicated sensor — only ABS sensors and module software

For wholesale buyers the practical takeaway is simple: stock direct-TPMS sensors for the models your customers actually service. Toyota, Nissan, Hyundai and Kia passenger cars sold across the Middle East, Africa, Latin America and Southeast Asia overwhelmingly use direct systems with replaceable sensor units, which is why those four brands form the core of the Kingmay TPMS catalog.

315 MHz vs 433 MHz: Matching Frequency to Destination Market

TPMS sensors transmit on one of two radio bands, and the frequency is fixed by the vehicle's body control module — a 433 MHz sensor will never pair with a 315 MHz car. Buying the wrong band is the most expensive mistake a first-time TPMS importer makes, because it only shows up after the customer has mounted the tires.

Because the same Corolla or Tucson can carry either band depending on where it was originally sold, the practical rule for distributors in mixed markets is to stock both frequencies in the top ten references and verify the band against the vehicle VIN or the existing sensor part number before shipping. Failure Diagnosis: When to Replace TPMS Sensors

Most TPMS complaints trace back to four root causes. Training workshop customers to diagnose before replacing protects their margins and prevents warranty claims on healthy units.

FAQ: TPMS Sensor Sourcing from China

Can I mix 315 MHz and 433 MHz sensors in one order?

Yes. Mixed-frequency containers are standard practice for distributors serving regions where both bands circulate — the Gulf, East Africa and Latin America all run 315 MHz on newer imports and 433 MHz on European-market vehicles. Kingmay packs each frequency in clearly marked cartons and lists the split on the packing list so destination customs clearance stays clean.

How do I verify which frequency a customer's vehicle uses?

Two reliable methods. First, check the existing sensor part number through the valve stem — the number is printed on the sensor body and maps directly to a frequency. Second, match the vehicle VIN or model-year market: North America, GCC and China-market vehicles are almost always 315 MHz, while European, Russian, most African and Southeast Asian market vehicles are 433 MHz. When in doubt, ask the customer to read the number off an existing sensor before ordering.

Do programmable TPMS sensors need a special tool to install?

The tool is needed to write the vehicle protocol into the blank sensor before fitting, not to mount the sensor itself. The programming step takes about 30 seconds per sensor with a handheld tool. Workshops that already own a TPMS diagnostic tool usually have programming built in; those that do not can add the Kingmay handheld tool at container-tier pricing, which is why most wholesale orders include one or two tools per pallet of sensors.

What is the typical battery life of a TPMS sensor?

Five to ten years of real-world service, depending on how often the vehicle is driven and the climate. High ambient heat shortens lithium battery life, which is why sensors in GCC vehicles often fail at the five-year mark while the same reference in a temperate climate runs past eight years. The battery is sealed inside the sensor body and is not field-serviceable, so the replacement unit is the service part.

Are aftermarket TPMS sensors as reliable as OE units?

OE-grade aftermarket units from a qualified factory match the OE pressure range, transmission protocol and battery specification, and are validated against the same relearn procedures. The differences from genuine-packaged parts are packaging, branding and price — typically 40-60% lower at wholesale. For independent repair shops and distributors, OE-grade aftermarket is the standard choice; genuine-packaged units are sourced for dealership customers who require original boxes.

What documents come with a wholesale TPMS order?

Each shipment includes a commercial invoice, packing list, certificate of origin and a pre-shipment inspection report with photos. Sensors ship as HS 8531.90 or 9031.80 depending on destination, and Kingmay labels cartons with frequency, part number and quantity for straightforward customs clearance. Radio-frequency certification documents (CE for 433 MHz, FCC for 315 MHz) are available on request for regulated markets.

The XPENG G9 sits at the top of XPENG's SUV range, and the 2026 facelift launched on January 8 gives exporters a flagship electric SUV that undercuts European premium badges by a wide margin. The updated car brought a new Turing AI chip, a switch to 5C lithium iron phosphate chemistry, and charging figures that still lead the segment. For dealers in the Gulf, Latin America and Southeast Asia, it is a showroom piece that doubles as a technology demonstration for the whole Chinese EV category.

This guide walks through the 2026 lineup and its verified specifications, how the 800V platform behaves on non-Chinese charging networks, which driver-assistance features survive export, FOB pricing tiers, landed cost in five markets, and the battery documentation customs officers ask for.

Why the 2026 G9 Facelift Matters for Importers

The original G9 launched in 2022 with one of the first mass-production 800V silicon-carbide platforms. The 2026 car keeps that foundation and adds three things buyers actually notice: a 5C-rate LFP battery that accepts up to 530 kW at compatible stations, a cabin built on the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8295P with dual 14.96-inch 2.4K screens, and a driver-assistance stack rated at 750 TOPS per Turing chip with up to three chips fitted on the top package.

Chinese retail pricing starts at RMB 248,800 for the 625 Max and reaches RMB 278,800 for the 680 AWD Max before incentives. Even after freight and duties, the G9 lands in most markets well below a similarly equipped German mid-size electric SUV, which is exactly why fleet buyers and premium used-car dealers keep adding it to orders.

The 2026 range is simple: two rear-wheel-drive versions and one dual-motor AWD flagship. Body dimensions are shared across trims at 4,891 mm long, 1,937 mm wide, 1,670 mm tall, on a 2,998 mm wheelbase.

Top speed is 200 km/h, and an optional electrically folding tow bar is rated at 1,500 kg. The boot holds up to 1,795 litres with seats folded.

Inside, every 2026 car gets Nappa leather with heating, ventilation and a ten-point massage program for both front seats, rear backrests that electrically recline from 27 to 37 degrees, a 20-speaker Xopera 7.1.4 audio system, and a streaming rear-view mirror.

800V SEPA 2.0 Platform & 5C Charging: What Works Abroad

The headline number is 10-80% in about 12 minutes at a compatible 5C liquid-cooled station, with peak DC input up to 530 kW on the long-range and AWD versions (445 kW on the standard pack). The X-HP 3.0 thermal system pre-conditions the pack and lets the car accept full power in ambient temperatures from -30°C to 50°C, which matters for Gulf summers and Central Asian winters alike.

The practical caveat for importers: 5C-class chargers are still rare outside China. On a typical 350 kW European- or GCC-standard CCS2 dispenser, independent tests of the G9 recorded around 200 kW real-world input, which still refills roughly 200 km of range in five minutes and 10-80% in the low twenties of minutes. The car's onboard boost logic also lets it charge at full speed on older 400V stations without adapters, so no destination market leaves the G9 stranded - it just will not hit the brochure numbers until local ultra-fast networks mature.

Turing AI Chip & XNGP: Region-Locked ADAS Reality

Every 2026 G9 carries at least one Turing AI chip (750 TOPS); the optional Ultra package adds a second and third chip for 2,250 TOPS total and runs the second-generation VLA (visual-language-action) model. Full-scenario City NOA, park-to-park navigation assistance, automatic emergency steering, and AEB rated to 130 km/h are all part of the stack.

Export buyers need to plan around two facts. First, XNGP's high-level functions are trained and licensed for Chinese roads; on export units the practical feature set is the highway pilot, adaptive cruise, lane keeping and the full passive-safety AEB suite, with urban NOA inactive until XPENG enables it in a given country. Second, map and telematics services (voice assistant, online navigation) depend on local connectivity. Resellers should advertise the G9 on its hardware, charging speed and driving dynamics - not on promises of full urban autonomy - to avoid after-sales disputes.

Color, Options & Configuration Notes for Export Orders

The 2026 palette comprises Pearl White, Midnight Black, Nebula White, Interstellar Green and the new Crescent Silver matte. Matte paint carries a surcharge and needs a paint-correction polishing kit packed in the container, because most destination-market detailers have limited experience with matte clear coats. Two appearance bundles change the car's retail story: the blacked-out package (dark trim, dark wheels, tinted glass) photographs well for social-media-driven dealerships, while the Moonlight Knight package pairs the matte silver paint with chrome deletes for buyers targeting the premium end of the used-car market.

On the chip package, the standard single Turing chip covers everything most export markets can legally use today. The two- and three-chip Ultra packages add nothing to highway-pilot behavior outside China yet, but they future-proof the car for markets where XPENG plans software rollouts through its joint ventures. Buyers in the UAE, Australia and Southeast Asia should weigh the package cost against a possible paid upgrade path later; buyers in markets with no announced XPENG presence should take the standard chip and put the difference into the air-suspension-equipped AWD trim instead, because ride quality is what customers feel on day one.

Inspection points before balance payment: verify the tow bar is physically fitted if ordered (it is a factory-fit item that cannot be retrofitted locally), run a dead-pixel scan on both 14.96-inch displays and the streaming mirror, and confirm the charging inlet matches the destination standard. China-market units use the GB/T connector, so adapter strategy must be settled at order time - for most markets we pre-install the destination-standard inlet on special-order vehicles, which avoids the 3-5% charging-efficiency loss and the warranty questions that third-party adapters raise.

Battery Certification & Pre-Shipment Paperwork

Electric vehicles clear customs on their battery documents. Before any G9 leaves the yard, confirm the pack ships with: UN38.3 test summary (the eight-abuse test series for lithium cells), a battery packing instruction statement referencing PI 965 section IA/IB where cells ship separately, MSDS/SDS in English, and the state-of-charge certificate keeping the pack at or below 30% SoC for sea freight under IMDG Code special provision 376.

Destination-specific extras: GCC-type approval paperwork (GSO) for Gulf markets, ADR exemption documentation where dangerous-goods rules apply to inland transport, and the energy-label or homologation files Australia and Chile require for registration. We provide the full document pack digitally before the vessel sails and physically with the B/L set, which is usually the difference between a two-day and a two-week customs release.

Ordering & Shipping Workflow from Nansha

The standard sequence runs: confirm trim, color and chip package; pay the 30% deposit; production allocation within 2-4 weeks; pre-shipment inspection with a photo/video report and third-party inspection certificate if requested; balance payment against documents; RoRo sailing from Nansha or container loading at Nansha/Guangzhou ports. Transit times run roughly 18-22 days to Jebel Ali, 25-30 days to Melbourne, 30-35 days to San Antonio, and 12-15 days to Manila.

Spare-parts support follows the vehicle: filters, brake components, body panels and battery-service documentation are stocked in Guangzhou, and we consolidate parts containers with vehicle orders so dealers do not carry a second freight bill.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the real charging speed of the 2026 G9 outside China?

On 5C-class 800V stations, 10-80% in about 12 minutes. On common 350 kW CCS2 dispensers abroad, expect roughly 200 kW real-world input, which still means 10-80% in the low twenties of minutes. The car boosts on older 400V networks without adapters, so it charges everywhere - just not always at brochure speed.

Does XNGP driver assistance work after export?

Urban NOA and park-to-park functions are licensed for Chinese roads. Export units keep highway pilot, adaptive cruise, lane keeping and full AEB (rated to 130 km/h). Urban autonomy activates only where XPENG has enabled the service, so advertise the car on hardware and safety features rather than full self-driving claims.

What range should I quote customers - CLTC or WLTP?

Quote CLTC minus 15-20%. The 680 km AWD figure translates to roughly 540-580 km realistic mixed-use range, and 430-470 km in sustained summer heat with heavy air-conditioning. Fleet buyers should size charging around the conservative number.

Which battery documents does customs require?

UN38.3 test summary, MSDS/SDS in English, a packing-instruction statement, and a state-of-charge certificate at or below 30% for sea freight under IMDG SP376. Gulf markets additionally need GSO conformity paperwork. We ship the full pack with the B/L set.

What warranty applies to exported G9 units?

Chinese-market warranty is 5 years/120,000 km vehicle and 8 years/160,000 km for the battery, motor and control electronics. Warranty service outside China depends on XPENG's local network, so many export buyers purchase extended third-party coverage or negotiate parts-supply agreements alongside the vehicle contract.

Can I order left-hand-drive and right-hand-drive versions?

The G9 is built in LHD; RHD units for Australia and other Commonwealth markets are available through XPENG's export program on allocated production runs with longer lead times - typically 8-12 weeks from deposit. Confirm RHD allocation windows before committing to retail customers.

Steering linkage parts occupy a specific spot in every auto parts warehouse: low unit price, high turnover, and a direct line to workshop customers who need them every week. Potholes, overloading and rough rural roads chew through tie rod ends faster than almost any other chassis component, which is why distributors serving Africa, the Middle East and Southeast Asia treat rack ends and outer tie rod ends as core stock rather than occasional orders.

This guide separates the two parts that buyers most often confuse, lists verified OE numbers for the Hyundai, Kia, Toyota and Nissan applications that dominate export volume, and walks through thread specs, FOB pricing tiers and container loading from Guangzhou.

Why Steering Linkage Parts Never Sit on the Shelf

Three forces keep steering linkage moving year after year. First, every wheel alignment job starts with an inspection of the tie rods, so worn ends get flagged and replaced as a matter of routine. Second, ball studs and rack boots are exposed to water, dust and salt with no protection beyond a rubber boot, so they wear on schedule even when the driver is careful. Third, the parts are cheap enough that repair shops replace rather than rebuild — nobody presses a new ball stud into an old housing.

For a distributor, the buying pattern matters as much as the wear pattern. A typical first order is a mixed pallet of 50 to 200 pieces per SKU, then monthly replenishment once the workshop customer base settles. Steering linkage also pulls related sales: a customer replacing tie rods usually needs stabilizer links, ball joints and control arm bushings checked at the same time, so stocking the full front-end group increases the average order value. Our earlier guides cover the wider chassis group — see the suspension overview (id=80) and the shock absorber and strut mount guide (id=121).

Rack End vs Outer Tie Rod End: What Distributors Must Separate

The steering linkage has two replaceable joints per side. The rack end — also called the inner tie rod — screws directly into the steering rack shaft and carries the rack boot on its body. The outer tie rod end connects the rack end to the steering arm on the knuckle through a tapered ball stud. Turning the steering wheel pushes the rack, the rack end transmits that force, and the outer tie rod end pivots to follow the wheel as the suspension moves up and down.

Catalogs blur the naming: some list the rack end as an "inner tie rod end", others as a "rack end" or even "side rod". The mistake that costs money is treating them as interchangeable. They are not: the rack end has a long threaded shank and no taper stud, while the outer has a tapered stud with a castle nut or self-locking nut. When a buyer orders "tie rod ends" without specifying, the supplier has to guess — and a mixed container of wrong parts is expensive to unwind. Always order by OE number and position, and if you cannot read the OE from the old part, send a photo of the removed piece plus the vehicle make, model, year and engine.

Product photo: Kingmay Auto Parts

Failure Symptoms Your Workshop Customers Report First

Steering linkage wear announces itself in a predictable sequence, and knowing the symptoms helps you advise customers and upsell the paired part:

  • Loose or vague steering. The wheel turns a few degrees before the car responds. This is the classic rack end wear signature as the ball stud develops play inside its seat.
  • Clunk or knock over bumps. A worn outer tie rod end knocks when the suspension cycles, especially on rough roads or speed bumps.
  • Front-end vibration. Play anywhere in the linkage lets the wheel shimmy at highway speed.
  • Uneven inner or outer tire wear. Steering play changes toe angle as the car rolls, feathering the tire edges.
  • Failed alignment. If toe cannot be held within spec, the tie rods are usually the culprit — the alignment rack finds the wear before the customer does.
  • Torn boot and grease loss. A split rack boot dries the rack end out within weeks. Replace the boot and the rack end together; greasing a worn joint buys a month at best.

The standard bench check: with the front wheel off the ground, rock the wheel at the 3 and 9 o'clock positions and watch the ball stud. Visible play means replacement. Play at the 12 and 6 o'clock positions points to a wheel bearing instead — a distinction worth teaching your workshop customers, because it protects you from warranty claims on parts that were not the fault.

Nissan adds a third digit in the suffix (D8520- vs D8570-) on heavier applications such as the Patrol. Quote both sides in every offer — workshops almost always change them in pairs.

Thread Specs & Dimensional Matching Before You Order

OE numbers settle fitment, but dimensions settle quality. Before confirming an order for any steering linkage SKU, lock these five measurements with the supplier against the old part or a dimensional sheet:

Ask every new supplier for that level of detail; suppliers who cannot produce it are reselling, not manufacturing.

Quality Checks Before Loading

Steering parts carry safety liability, so inspection deserves more rigor than price-tier parts get. Four checks catch most problems before the container sails:

  • Forging and material. Ball housings should be die-forged from 40Cr or 45# steel with visible forging flow lines, not castings. Cast ball housings crack under side load — ask for the material certificate alongside the sample.
  • Ball stud pull-off force. A serviceable joint must hold the stud under a measured axial load (documented in kN on the test report). Request the report for the production batch, not a generic datasheet.
  • Boot material and grease fill. EPDM or high-grade TPE boots resist cracking in desert heat; check the grease fill weight against spec — under-filled joints run dry and wear out early, which shows up as warranty claims in month four.
  • Thread and torque retention. Gauge-check the housing threads with a real nut on site, and confirm the stake or crimp that locks the bearing seat survives the specified torque.

Factories running IATF 16949 systems will hand over batch test reports without prompting. If a supplier resists, treat it as a screening answer and move on — the steering category is too liability-heavy to gamble on an unverified line.

Left/Right Pairing, MOQ & Container Loading

Plan inventory in pairs. A Tucson outer end order should arrive as 50 LH (56820-2E000) plus 50 RH (56820-2E900), not 100 of one side. Workshops replace both ends in one alignment job most of the time, and unbalanced stock ties up cash on the slow side. The same logic applies to Toyota 45047/45046 and Nissan D8520/D8570 pairs.

On loading: a standard mixed steering-linkage pallet holds 40 cartons of 60 pieces — roughly 2,400 mixed pieces per pallet, and a 40-ft high-cube container takes about 20 pallets, so a full container program covers 45,000–50,000 pieces across 20 to 30 SKUs. Keep the top ten fast movers (Tucson, Elantra, Corolla, Vios, Sentra ends) at two pallets each and let the long tail share the rest. Inner rack ends pack denser than outer ends, so mixed-pallet loading usually lands within 3% of the calculated volume.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between a rack end and an outer tie rod end?

The rack end (inner tie rod) screws into the steering rack shaft and carries the rack boot; the outer tie rod end bolts to the knuckle's steering arm with a tapered ball stud. They are separate parts with separate OE numbers and usually separate lifespans — the outer wears faster because it pivots with every wheel movement.

How do I know a tie rod end needs replacement?

Watch for loose steering, clunks over bumps, front-end vibration and uneven tire edge wear. On the bench, lift the wheel, rock it at the 3 and 9 o'clock positions and look for visible play at the ball stud. Any measurable play means the joint is done.

Should tie rod ends be replaced in pairs?

Yes in practice. Both sides have the same mileage and wear, workshops change both during one alignment session, and replacing in pairs keeps toe settings symmetric. Stock LH and RH in equal quantities.

Is wheel alignment required after replacing tie rod ends?

Always. Replacing an outer end changes the linkage length and moves the toe angle. Thread the new end to the marked position on the old part to get the car to the alignment shop, then set toe to factory spec.

What vehicles does OE 56820-2E000 fit?

It is the front-left outer tie rod end for the Hyundai Tucson (JM) and Kia Sportage II (JE/KM), 2004–2010, with 56820-2E900 as its right-hand pair. Cross-references include 555 SEK-8041L, CTR CEKH-35L and MOOG HY-ES-3887.

What is the MOQ and lead time for wholesale tie rod ends from China?

Sample batches ship in 5–7 days with no minimum beyond courier cost. Production orders start at 50 pieces per SKU, with tiered pricing at 200 and 1,000 pieces, and container orders run 25–35 days from deposit to port.

Two GWM nameplates cover opposite ends of the SUV export trade, and most wholesale enquiries end up needing both. The Haval H6 sells on price and equipment against RAV4-class rivals, while the Haval H9 answers the question fleet buyers in Russia, the Gulf and Africa ask most often: which China-built SUV survives towing, desert tracks and broken asphalt without paying a Japanese body-on-frame price? This guide sets out the 2026 Haval H6 export price ladder, the H9 diesel export specifications that matter in fleet tenders, and the market-by-market fit that decides which model belongs in your order.

All prices quoted are FOB Nansha, Guangzhou, based on 2026 model-year quotations for left-hand-drive units. RHD production for the H9 is available on order; the H6 is built in LHD only for most export trims, which shapes where each model can be sold.

Why the H6 and H9 Belong in the Same Export Order

GWM shipped Haval-branded SUVs to more than 170 markets in 2025, and the two models anchor opposite ends of that trade. The H6 is the volume play: a 2,738 mm wheelbase family SUV priced against Corolla Cross and Tucson, sold to distributors who need turnover and warranty depth. The H9 is the margin play: a 5.0 m ladder-frame SUV with low-range 4WD that competes where Fortuner and Land Cruiser Prado prices have climbed past what many markets can absorb.

For a distributor, the pairing matters because the two models share a dealer support structure — the same parts catalogues, the same training material and the same diagnostic platform. A market entrant can open with 20 H6 units for retail turnover and add H9 stock for the mining, security and government fleet segments that pay premium margins. Importers in Kazakhstan, Nigeria and Saudi Arabia all run this two-tier structure; our earlier guides cover the Chery equivalent (Tiggo 8 Pro / Tiggo 9 for Russia and Central Asia) and the Jetour equivalent (Jetour Traveler 4WD).

Haval H6 2026: Engine, Trim and Equipment Overview

The fourth-generation H6 facelift carries three powertrains into 2026. The 1.5T is the fleet workhorse — 135 kW through a 7-speed wet dual-clutch, returning 6.8 L/100 km on the WLTC cycle. The 2.0T adds 175 kW and an on-demand AWD system for markets with hills, gravel or towing duty. The HEV pairs the 1.5T with a front-mounted P1+P2 hybrid module and a 1.8 kWh battery, cutting urban consumption below 5.5 L/100 km without charging infrastructure.

Equipment on export trims runs at the high end of the class: 14.6-inch centre screen, wireless CarPlay and Android Auto on 2026 software, heated seats, a 540-degree camera on upper trims and six airbags across the range. ADAS content (AEB, adaptive cruise, lane keeping) is standard on 2.0T and HEV trims and optional on the 1.5T base. Build quality for Russia and CIS-spec units includes an engine block heater and cold-climate battery; Gulf-spec units add upgraded AC capacity and dust sealing. The table below compares the four export powertrains across the H6 and H9 ranges.

Haval H9 2026: Body-on-Frame Diesel and Petrol for Hard Duty

The second-generation H9 moved to a ladder frame with a double-wishbone front and solid-axle rear suspension, and that chassis choice decides which buyers order it. TOD (Torque-On-Demand) 4WD with a 2.48:1 low-range transfer case is standard on both engines; the flagship diesel trim adds a rear differential lock. Approach and departure angles of 30 and 26 degrees put it in the same envelope as the Fortuner, well clear of any monocoque SUV at this price.

Export buyers split between the two engines in a predictable pattern. The 2.0T petrol suits Gulf and Central Asian markets where diesel quality varies and petrol infrastructure is universal. The 2.4T diesel is the specification of choice for Russian tenders, African mining fleets and any buyer who clocks highway kilometres — the 80-litre tank and 8.6 L/100 km give a real 850 km range between fills, which matters where fuel stations are 200 km apart. Seating is five or seven depending on market homologation; most African and Russian stock ships as five-seat with a flat-load cargo floor.

FOB Nansha Price List and Order Tiers

The 2026 Haval H6 export price ladder and H9 pricing are set out below. These are indicative FOB Nansha figures for LHD units at container tier; volume and trim selection move the final quotation, and RHD commands a 4-6% premium on the H9.

Container loading uses wheel-frame racks: four H6 units per 40HC is standard practice, and two H9 units per container with the boot-to-boot method. RORO is the better option above eight units per sailing — Nansha has direct car-carrier sailings to the Gulf (18-22 days to Jebel Ali), West Africa (25-35 days to Lagos) and Russia (Far East lines via Vladivostok, Black Sea lines to Novorossiysk), while Central Asia moves by rail through Khorgos in 18-22 days. The Haval H6 hybrid FOB Nansha price of $19,800 is the number most fleet buyers compare against Corolla Cross Hybrid quotations, which currently start around $24,000 at the same port.

Russia and Central Asia: Certification and the Tula Question

Russia remains the largest Haval export market by volume, and buyers should understand how the local plant changes the trade. GWM builds the H6, Jolion, Dargo and H3 at its Tula factory, so domestically-produced supply covers those models. The H9 is not built at Tula — China-built units carry the entire market, which is why the diesel H9 holds its resale value unusually well there. Importing the H6 into Russia competes with Tula output and customs duty, so the practical Russian order book is H9-heavy.

Customs documentation workflow for China-built vehicle imports into Russia and the EAEU.

Certification runs through the EAC system under TR CU 018/2011, with single-vehicle type approval (OTTC/SBKTS) handled per unit for parallel imports and SBKTS-registered clearance for commercial lots. Budget three paperwork items that catch first-time importers: the utilization fee (raised again in 2025 for commercial importers), power-based excise on the petrol H9, and GLONASS-era emergency system requirements. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan accept the same EAC framework with lower utilization fees, which is why many CIS traders clear stock through Almaty before re-export. Our Russia GOST/EAC certification guide walks through the full document chain.

Middle East and Africa Fit: Heat, Dust and Fuel Quality

Gulf buyers order the H6 2.0T and petrol H9. Both engines carry upgraded cooling and AC specifications for 50°C ambient operation, and the petrol choice avoids the diesel-particulate complications that 45°C stop-start city traffic creates. Saudi fleet tenders increasingly specify the H6 HEV for municipal and airport duty where fuel subsidy reform has shifted the running-cost calculation.

GWM Haval wholesale to the Africa market leans the other way. Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana and Tanzania take the 1.5T H6 for urban retail and the diesel H9 for upcountry, mining and NGO duty. Two spec decisions matter on African orders: fit the full-size spare as standard (the H9 already carries one; spec it on the H6 fleet trim), and confirm the fuel program — both engines run on 91 RON, but markets with uncertain fuel quality should order the petrol H6 with the standard (non-GDi) injection calibration, which tolerates variation better. Parts support runs through the same Kingmay-serviced channel as other Chinese brands; a front-end parts set for the H6 costs roughly a third of the Fortuner equivalent.

H9 vs Toyota Fortuner and Pajero Sport

The H9's real competition is not the Chinese market — it is the used and new Fortuner trade. The comparison below sets the diesel H9 against the two ladder-frame rivals that dominate Gulf and African tender lists.

The decision usually comes down to resale depth versus acquisition cost. The Fortuner sells faster at trade-in and its parts network is unmatched; the H9 undercuts it by $12,000-20,000 per unit landed, carries more equipment as standard, and the Pajero Sport's exit from production has left tender buyers searching for a mid-price ladder-frame alternative — a gap the diesel H9 fills directly. For traders, the margin sits in the price gap; for end fleets, the calculation is depreciation against purchase price.

Landed Cost Snapshots for Four Markets

Landed cost decides which variant wins each order, so the two most-quoted builds are set out below with indicative duty, freight and tax components. Figures use 2026 RORO and container rates and should be treated as planning estimates, not quotations.

H6 1.5T (FOB $14,600) — retail-market build:

  • UAE (Jebel Ali): 5% duty $730 + RORO freight ~$1,700 + 5% VAT on CIF → landed ≈ $17,900
  • Nigeria (Lagos): duty and levies ≈ 40% ($6,200) + freight ~$2,600 → landed ≈ $23,600 before port charges
  • Kazakhstan (rail, Khorgos): EAEU duty 15% ($2,190) + rail freight ~$2,400 + VAT → landed ≈ $20,300

H9 2.4T diesel (FOB $31,500) — fleet build:

  • UAE (Jebel Ali): 5% duty $1,575 + freight ~$1,700 + VAT → landed ≈ $36,100
  • Russia (Novorossiysk): 15% duty + 20% VAT + power-based excise + utilization fee + freight ~$3,400 → landed ≈ $43,500
  • Australia (Melbourne): 0% duty under ChAFTA + 10% GST on CIF + freight ~$2,200 → landed ≈ $37,000 before ADR/RAWS compliance

Two notes on the snapshots. Nigeria's effective charge on new vehicles is the steepest of the four, which is why H6 stock there concentrates in the fleet trim and why used-Japanese competition stays strong below $20,000. Australia's zero duty under ChAFTA is a genuine advantage, but RAWS type-approval cost per model means H9 imports only pay off above 15-20 units per year — which suits established GWM dealers rather than first-time entrants.

Ordering Process, Lead Time and Mixed Loading

A first GWM order through our desk follows six steps: variant and trim confirmation against your market's homologation requirements, proforma invoice with FOB or CIF terms, 30% deposit, production slot booking (3-5 weeks if the trim is not in port stock), pre-shipment inspection with photo report, and balance against shipping documents. Units currently in Nansha stock ship within 10 days of deposit.

Mixed loading keeps first orders low-risk. A typical trial container pairs two H6 units with a parts package — filters, brake pads, suspension bushings and body panels sized to the retail forecast — so the dealer opens with both sales stock and service stock in one clearance. RORO bookings accept single units, which suits the H9 flagship trims that move slowly but at high margin. Warranty terms run five years or 150,000 km on most export markets with the parts programme supported from our Guangzhou warehouse; the products catalogue lists current H6/H9 fast-moving parts alongside the wider Chinese-brand coverage.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the 2026 Haval H6 export price from China?

The H6 range runs $14,600 for the 1.5T fleet trim, $17,900 for the 2.0T AWD and $19,800 for the HEV, all FOB Nansha at container tier. The H9 spans $28,800 (2.0T petrol) to $33,400 (diesel flagship with rear locker). Volume discounts of 2-4% apply above ten units per order, and RHD H9 units carry a 4-6% premium.

Can the Haval H9 be imported into Russia, and which certification applies?

Yes — the H9 is not produced at GWM's Tula plant, so China-built units supply the Russian market in full. Imports clear under the EAC framework (TR CU 018/2011) with OTTC or SBKTS per-unit approval, plus the 2025-raised utilization fee and power-based excise on the petrol version. The diesel H9's 2,393 cc keeps excise in a lower band than the petrol 2.0T's output would suggest at similar price points.

Is the Haval H6 hybrid suitable for African fuel quality?

The HEV runs 91 RON and tolerates moderate fuel variation, but where fuel quality is unpredictable we recommend the standard 1.5T or 2.0T with non-GDi injection calibration — fewer sensors, no high-voltage battery exposure to rough loading, and cheaper field repairs. The H6 hybrid FOB Nansha price makes sense for urban fleet tenders in Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana where running-cost clauses reward the 5.5 L/100 km city figure.

H9 vs Toyota Fortuner — which is cheaper to import?

The diesel H9 lands $12,000-20,000 below a new Fortuner 2.8 in the same market: roughly $36,100 landed in the UAE against $48,000-56,000 for the Fortuner, and the gap widens in Africa. The Fortuner's advantages are resale depth and parts ubiquity; the H9 answers with lower acquisition cost, more standard equipment and a 480 N·m diesel matched to the Fortuner's torque curve.

What is the minimum order and lead time from Nansha Port?

RORO accepts single units; container orders run from two H9 or four H6 per 40HC with mixed H6+H9 loading available. In-stock trims ship 10 days after deposit; factory orders take 3-5 weeks production plus transit — 18-22 days to Jebel Ali, 25-35 to Lagos, 18-22 by rail to Central Asia via Khorgos, and 30-45 days to Far East Russian ports depending on sailing schedules.

Does Australia charge import duty on China-built Haval SUVs?

No. Under the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement, passenger vehicles built in China enter at 0% duty; only 10% GST on the CIF value applies. The practical barrier is compliance — ADR approval through the Registered Automotive Workshop Scheme costs $8,000-15,000 per model variant, which is why H9 imports to Australia suit established GWM dealers moving 15-20+ units per year rather than one-off imports.

Quick Answer: Wholesale sourcing guide for Hyundai Santa Fe and Kia Sorento auto parts — brake pads and discs, suspension and cooling — covering every generation from the Santa Fe SM (2000) to the Sorento UM (2015–2020), with verified OE cross-reference tables, FOB Guangzhou price tiers by order volume, a quality grade comparison and landed cost examples for Kenya, the UAE and Saudi Arabia.

The Santa Fe and the Sorento are the two Hyundai-Kia SUVs that appear most often on the order sheets of importers serving the Gulf, Africa and Southeast Asia. Both are large family SUVs that get used hard: seven seats filled, roof racks loaded, trailers pulled, and outside temperatures that punish every cooling loop in the engine bay. That usage pattern chews through brake pads, eats suspension bushings and keeps radiators on the wanted list year-round — which is exactly why Santa Fe and Sorento parts wholesale volume from China holds steady even when broader import demand dips.

This guide maps the generations, lists the OE numbers our order books see most for brakes, suspension and cooling, and sets out FOB Guangzhou pricing tiers, quality grade differences and the landed cost math for three reference markets. If you buy Hyundai or Kia SUV parts for resale, this is the article to keep open when your supplier asks for the next purchase order.

Why Santa Fe & Sorento Parts Never Sit on the Shelf

Three things make these two nameplates fast movers. First, the combined parc is enormous: the Santa Fe has been in continuous production since 2000 and the Sorento since 2002, across five and four generations respectively, and both were sold in volume in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, Russia and across Central Asia. Second, both sit in the 1.7–2.0 tonne class — heavy enough to wear front brake pads in 40,000–60,000 km and stress front suspension under full load. Third, in Gulf markets these SUVs run air conditioning continuously in 45 °C heat, and a marginal cooling system becomes a failed water pump or a cracked radiator tank with no warning.

For distributors the buying pattern is predictable: brake pads every month, suspension parts every quarter, cooling parts as seasonal spikes before summer. Buyers who stock the three systems together capture the full repair order instead of half of it. Our earlier guides go deeper on each system — the Hyundai-Kia brake parts comparison covers ceramic versus semi-metallic friction materials, and the summer cooling guide covers the wider hot-climate cooling catalog.

Generation Map: Order by Chassis Code, Not by Year

The single most expensive mistake in this category is ordering "2012 Santa Fe pads" without the chassis code, because generation overlaps confuse year-based ordering. Hyundai and Kia catalog these vehicles by internal platform codes, and parts pricing, fitment and even the number of piston calipers change between them.

  • Santa Fe SM (2000–2006) — first generation, 2.7 V6 petrol focus, many still running in Africa as cheap family transport.
  • Santa Fe CM (2006–2012) — the volume generation for export parts; 2.4 petrol, 2.7 V6 and 2.2 CRDi diesel variants.
  • Santa Fe DM (2013–2018) — sharper styling, Theta-II GDI engines, larger front discs.
  • Santa Fe TM (2019–2023) and MX5 (2024–) — current platforms; TM parts demand is now climbing as these vehicles exit lease fleets.
  • Sorento BL (2002–2009) — body-on-frame first generation, popular in the Gulf as a tow vehicle.
  • Sorento XM (2009–2014) and UM (2015–2020) — unibody generations that share suspension architecture with the Santa Fe DM in several assemblies.
  • Sorento MQ4 (2021–) — current generation; hybrid variants increasingly common in Gulf fleets.
Ordering rule: always specify OE number plus chassis code, and flag 2WD versus 4WD. On the Santa Fe CM and Sorento XM, the 4WD front lower control arm (54500-2P000) is a different part from the 2WD arm (54500-2B000) — mixing them in one order is the most common cross-contamination error we see from first-time buyers.

Stocking to that pattern keeps your order book aligned with how the parts actually fail.

Material choice follows climate and customer. Ceramic compound runs quieter and produces less dust — Gulf customers with new vehicles ask for it by name. Semi-metallic handles heat cycling better on loaded diesel SUVs and costs 20–25% less, which is why fleet buyers in Africa and Central Asia standardize on it. Our brake system guide covers the friction material trade-offs in more detail.

Suspension Parts That Fail First on Loaded SUVs

Suspension wear on these platforms follows a sequence, and stocking to the sequence prevents dead inventory. Stabilizer links fail first — the small joints crack on rough roads within 60,000–80,000 km. Front shock absorbers follow, weeping oil after sustained hot, loaded running. Lower control arm bushings and ball joints degrade in parallel with the shocks, and strut mounts fail with the shocks they sit on. Rear suspension on both nameplates holds up well, but trailing arm bushings soften over time on towing Sorentos.

Material checks matter more here than on brakes because suspension parts carry load continuously. Ball joints and control arm forgings should be 40Cr or 45# steel with visible forging lines, not castings; bushings should be natural rubber for comfort markets or upgraded polyurethane where rough-road fleets dominate. Ask the supplier for batch pull-off test data on ball studs before the first container — the report separates manufacturers from resellers faster than any factory audit video.

Cooling Parts for Hot-Climate Markets

Cooling is the system where climate decides your stock list. A Santa Fe or Sorento running Gulf summers in stop-go traffic with a full load needs every watt of cooling capacity the radiator, fan and pump can deliver, and marginal parts fail exactly when the customer needs them most. The OE numbers our order books confirm for the volume generations:

On radiator construction: the OE-standard aluminium-plastic design (aluminium core, plastic tanks) is correct for the replacement market and keeps the price point where distributors need it. Verify core thickness and row count against the application — a thin-core economizer version will pass a bench test and still overheat in a 48 °C July in Riyadh. Every radiator in a Kingmay order gets a pressure test before packing, and we recommend buyers specify the test certificate on the first order from any new supplier.

On the 2.2 CRDi Santa Fe, a weeping pump seal found early saves the customer a front cover job later, which is why workshops quote pumps preventively above 120,000 km.

What brake pads fit a Hyundai Santa Fe?

It depends on the generation. The volume applications are front pad set 58101-2BA00 for the Santa Fe CM (2006–2012), 58101-4ZA00 for the DM (2013–2018) and 58101-2WA00 for the TM (2019–2023). Order by OE number plus chassis code — never by year alone, because generation overlaps at the borders.

In order: stabilizer links (60,000–80,000 km on rough roads), front shock absorbers (weeping oil after hot, loaded running), then control arm bushings, ball joints and strut mounts. Quick Answer: The A/C compressor is the fastest-wearing HVAC component in hot-climate fleets — at 45–50 °C ambient the condenser side runs near its pressure limit, and a clogged condenser or worn clutch can take the whole system down. China's OEM-grade tier supplies compressors for Toyota (88310/88320 series), Hyundai and Kia (97701 series) at indicative FOB Guangzhou prices of $85–350, with condensers from $28 and blower motors from $18. This guide maps the OE references across Toyota, Hyundai, Kia and Chinese EV platforms, explains belt-driven versus electric compressors and R134a vs R1234yf compatibility, and covers FOB pricing, container loading, the seven pre-shipment QC checks and the stocking calendar that decides whether your compressors land before or after the January–April peak.

Ask any workshop owner in Dubai, Riyadh or Lagos which repair generates the most customer anger in summer, and the answer is rarely brakes or suspension. It is air conditioning that quit in July. The part at the center of that failure is almost always the AC compressor — and for parts distributors serving the Gulf, Africa and South Asia, it is the single highest-stakes SKU in the climate control category. Getting AC compressor wholesale sourcing right from China means matching OE references precisely, understanding refrigerant compatibility, and timing the order so stock arrives before the season, not after it.

This guide is written for auto air conditioning parts suppliers, regional distributors and fleet maintenance buyers sourcing from China. It covers the OE number map for Toyota, Hyundai and Kia platforms, the supporting components that fail alongside the compressor, the belt-driven versus electric compressor split created by Chinese EV exports, refrigerant compatibility, indicative FOB pricing, quality control and the hot-climate stocking calendar. For the Korean-nameplate deep dive, our Hyundai Kia AC compressor and HVAC parts guide lists 19 additional OE references with fleet mix estimates.

Why Hot-Climate Markets Consume Compressors Faster

A compressor sized for a European summer works overtime in the Gulf. When ambient temperature reaches 48 °C — a normal July afternoon in Kuwait or interior Saudi Arabia — the high-side pressure on an R134a system climbs toward 25–29 bar, close to the relief valve threshold. The compressor spends long stretches at maximum displacement, shaft seals run hot, and the electromagnetic clutch slips more on every engagement. Field data from regional workshops consistently shows compressor replacement rates in GCC markets running roughly three times those of temperate climates, with the peak clustered in the months after the hottest quarter.

The failure chain usually starts upstream of the compressor itself. Desert dust and insects clog condenser fins, airflow drops, head pressure rises, and the compressor is the component that pays the price. That is why experienced distributors do not sell compressors alone: they pair every compressor with a new receiver-drier, push a condenser flush or replacement as an upsell, and quote the whole job. A workshop that replaces a $120 compressor and reuses a saturated drier is buying a comeback claim — moisture in the system reacts with refrigerant oil, forms acids, and kills the replacement compressor within months.

For a wholesale program, this failure pattern has a commercial consequence: climate control is a kit business, not a single-SKU business. The distributors who anchor their orders on compressors and then fill the container with condensers, driers, expansion valves and blower motors capture the whole repair ticket — and see far fewer warranty claims on the compressors they do sell.

Every serious air conditioning order starts with OE references. A "2019 Camry" does not define a compressor; the engine and production market do. Second, on the Toyota side, the 88310 and 88320 prefixes both mean compressor, but 88320 generally marks the newer scroll generation; quoting a 88310 number for a car that takes a 88320 unit is the most common ordering mistake we see from first-time buyers. Beyond the Compressor: The Full Climate Control Kit

The compressor gets the shelf space, but the ticket is won on the supporting cast. A complete hot-climate stocking program covers six component families, and each has its own failure logic:

  • Condensers — parallel-flow aluminum cores; the first thing desert dust chokes. Sell coated fins for coastal humidity.
  • Receiver-driers / accumulator-desiccants — replace with every compressor; stock three times as many as you think you need.
  • Expansion valves and orifice tubes — small, cheap, and the cause of many misdiagnosed "bad compressor" complaints.
  • Blower motors and resistors — the 97113 series covers Hyundai and Kia platforms broadly (97113-C1000 fits Tucson TL and Sportage SL); PWM variants like 97235-A8000 serve newer cars.
  • Pressure switches and sensors — the low-charge cutout that protects the compressor; a $6 part that saves a $120 one.
  • Hose assemblies and O-ring kits — crimped hose failures spike in heat; HNBR O-rings survive R134a service at Gulf temperatures where standard NBR does not.

Kit economics are straightforward: a compressor-condenser-drier-valve kit quotes at roughly 1.8–2.2× the compressor alone but converts a one-line order into a four-line order and locks the workshop out of your competitors for that repair. We quote HVAC programs as kits by default — see our Hyundai Kia cooling system guide for how the engine-cooling half of the same container is built.

Belt-Driven vs Electric: Sourcing for Mixed Fleets and Chinese EVs

Chinese vehicle exports have added a second compressor technology to every distributor's price list. Conventional cars and PHEVs run belt-driven compressors off the engine; battery-electric vehicles have no engine crankshaft to belt onto, so they run electric compressors — a sealed motor-pump unit fed from the high-voltage DC bus. BYD, Geely, GAC and other Chinese EV export platforms all use them, and the sourcing logic is different in almost every dimension that matters.

Two sourcing consequences follow. First, electric compressors are platform-locked in a way belt units never were — a BYD e-compressor reference will not cross to a Geely, so stocking depth matters more than breadth; a distributor serving Chinese EV fleets should pick the two or three platforms their market actually runs (from our Chinese EV parts sourcing guide) and go deep. Second, the 800 V platforms appearing on newer EVs raise insulation requirements; buyers should insist on hipot test reports for every electric compressor batch, a test most economical-tier factories simply do not run.

R134a vs R1234yf: Refrigerant Compatibility When Stocking

Refrigerant generation is the invisible line that separates usable stock from shelf-rotting stock. The global fleet split is stable: virtually all Toyota, Hyundai and Kia vehicles on Gulf, African and South Asian roads run R134a, while EU-market vehicles from 2017 onward and a growing share of US-market cars run R1234yf (lower global-warming potential, higher refrigerant price, different service fittings and compressor oil). Chinese export-market vehicles overwhelmingly specify R134a as well.

Three practical rules for a wholesale program. One: never quote a compressor into an R1234yf application using R134a oil charge — the POE oil in yf systems is not interchangeable with the PAG oil in 134a systems, and a mismatched charge converts a correct compressor into a callback. Two: check the service port before quoting; yf ports are different-sized by regulation precisely to prevent cross-charging, and a photo of the port settles the question in seconds. Three: stock R134a parts deep and R1234yf parts narrow — for a Middle East or Africa distributor, yf applications are a small slice of the fleet today, but the EU-used-car export wave is starting to move yf vehicles into Gulf and African second markets, so a two-shelf yf trial program is cheap insurance.

What OEM-Grade Means for AC Parts — and the Certificates That Back It

"OEM-grade" in climate control is verifiable in four places. Certification first: a factory supplying the OE tier or its mirror holds IATF 16949 quality-system certification, and for Gulf-bound shipments the parts themselves carry GSO / SASO conformity documentation (Saudi Arabia's SABER platform requires a Certificate of Conformity per shipment); Kenya-bound stock needs a KEBS pre-export verification certificate. We build first orders as mixed-platform containers precisely so distributors can read their own turn-rate data before committing shelf depth — the same first-container strategy we apply to brake and suspension programs.

Quality Control: Seven Checks Before an AC Order Ships

A pre-shipment inspection for climate control is a functional test, not a box count. The seven checks we run or require:

  • Clutch engagement test — apply rated voltage, measure engagement gap and listen for drag; reject lots with inconsistent pull-in.
  • Shaft seal leak check — sniffer or pressure-decay test on every sampled compressor, not just the golden sample.
  • Rotation smoothness — hand-turn or low-speed run; grinding or notchy bearings are the single most common economical-tier defect.
  • Internal cleanliness and purge — confirm nitrogen charge holds and port caps are sealed; a hiss on opening is good news.
  • Condenser leak test certificates — 100% test record per batch, plus fin-coating adhesion for coated cores.
  • Fitment trial — pulley groove count, bracket bolt pattern and port orientation checked against a sample application or OE drawing.
  • Label and document audit — OE cross-reference printed, batch codes legible, GSO/SASO or KEBS documents matching the shipment.

Third-party inspection agencies execute this checklist at most Chinese HVAC factories for a standard man-day fee, and we coordinate it for buyers ordering through our Guangzhou program. The cost is trivial against the value of a container; the comeback claims it prevents are not.

The Hot-Climate Stocking Calendar

Timing decides whether HVAC stock sells at full margin or sits until next year. The demand curve in Gulf and African markets peaks from March through June and stays heavy through September — air conditioning is not a comfort purchase there, it is the reason the vehicle runs at all. Working backwards: workshops start stocking in January, regional distributors order in November–December, and factories need 20–30 days of production plus 18–28 days of ocean transit to Jebel Ali, Dammam or Mombasa.

That arithmetic puts early December as the last comfortable order date for a January arrival, and any order placed after mid-December should assume the first weeks of the peak season will be missed. Auto air conditioning parts suppliers who order compressors and condensers in October–November — right after this article publishes — consistently capture the season's first repair wave at full price, while late buyers spend the peak discounting stock that arrives in May. This year the calculus has one extra wrinkle: Red Sea routing adjustments have lengthened some Middle East transits, which moves the real order deadline earlier, not later.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the genuine OE numbers for Toyota AC compressors?

For the Camry XV40 generation, compressor 88310-33250; the Aurion and later Camry V40 series use 88320-33200; the RAV4 and Corolla family reference 88320-0E030 as the catalog item. Toyota supersedes numbers by production market, so confirm against the VIN before ordering a wholesale quantity.

Which OE references cover Hyundai and Kia AC compressors?

The 97701 series covers most applications: 97701-2S500 and 97701-1R000 for Elantra and Accent, 97701-3R200 for Sorento and Carnival platforms, and 97701-3K125 for Tucson and Sportage generations (VIN confirmation required). The same platform shares condensers in the 97606/97130 series and blower motors in the 97113 series.

How much does an OEM-grade AC compressor cost wholesale from China?

Indicative FOB Guangzhou pricing runs $85–350 for belt-driven compressors depending on platform and clutch configuration, and $220–600 for electric EV compressors, which are platform-specific. MOQs start at 10–30 pieces per reference in the OEM-grade tier.

Can I use R134a parts in an R1234yf system?

No. The systems use different refrigerants, different oils (PAG versus POE) and different service fittings by regulation. Supplying a 134a-charged compressor into a yf application converts a correct part into a warranty claim. Check the service port size or the under-hood label before quoting.

Do Chinese EVs use the same AC compressors as petrol cars?

No. Battery-electric vehicles use electric compressors driven from the high-voltage bus — no belt, no clutch — with stepless speed control. They are platform-locked (a BYD unit will not cross to a Geely) and require hipot insulation test reports for every batch, a check worth demanding from any supplier.

When should Middle East and Africa distributors place their AC compressor orders?

Order in October–November so production completes by December and containers land in January, ahead of the March–June repair peak. Early December is the last comfortable order date for a January arrival, and current Red Sea routing adjustments add transit time, which pushes the effective deadline earlier.

title: Pre-Shipment Inspection for Auto Parts Orders After Canton Fair
description: Where pre-shipment inspection fits between purchase order and container: AQL sample sizes, defect classes, category checklists, the written protocol and container loading supervision.
toc: Why the Risk Starts After the Fair Ends
Three Checkpoints, and Most Buyers Use Only One
AQL in Numbers You Will Actually See
Classify Defects Before Production Starts
What Gets Measured, by Category
The Written Protocol Decides the Dispute
Timing, and the Leverage You Have
Container Loading Supervision: The Step Buyers Skip
When to Skip It, and When to Run It Twice
Turning the Report into a Supplier Decision
Frequently Asked Questions
content:
The 140th Canton Fair put auto parts on the floor from 15 to 19 October and then took them away again: Phase 2 (23–27 October) is home goods and building materials, Phase 3 (31 October–4 November) is textiles and toys. Whatever you agreed at Pazhou now becomes a purchase order, a production slot and a container — and nothing you saw at the booth tells you what comes off the line in six weeks. Pre-shipment inspection is the only checkpoint that decides while the goods are still on the factory floor and the balance payment is still in your hands.

Why the Risk Starts After the Fair Ends

Booth samples are made when nobody is rushing. Production parts are made when the plant is running three shifts to clear a November backlog, a substitute material arrives late, or a sub-supplier changes because the original one was full. None of that is visible from a quotation.

The buyer who ordered at the fair typically signs a proforma invoice with a 30 percent deposit and a balance due against the bill of lading. Once that balance is paid, the leverage is gone: a defective container becomes a cross-border argument, a negotiated discount on the next order, or a write-off. The entire purpose of pre-shipment inspection is to move the decision to the point where it still costs the supplier something to be wrong.

Our supplier verification guide covers who you are buying from. This article covers what you do between the purchase order and the container.

Three Checkpoints, and Most Buyers Use Only One

Quality control in Chinese trade runs on three separate visits. They are not interchangeable.

CheckpointWhenWhat it catchesWhat it cannot catch
Pre-production / first-articleBefore the run, on the first off-tool partsWrong material, wrong tooling, wrong OE referenceDrift across a long run
During production (DUPRO)30–50 percent completeDimensional drift, coating thickness, a substitute componentAnything that happens in the second half
Pre-shipment (PSI)100 percent produced, at least 80 percent packedFinished-goods defects, quantity shortfall, packaging and labellingRoot causes — it is too late to fix the process

Importers who run only the third checkpoint describe a defect rate in the low single digits. Importers who add the first two routinely land below 0.1 percent, because a wrong friction compound found on day three is a material change, while the same compound found on day thirty is a rejected container. The extra visit costs one inspector-day; the alternative costs the shipment.

Container loading supervision is a fourth, separate activity — see section 8.

AQL in Numbers You Will Actually See

Acceptable Quality Limit is not a promise that the factory may ship that many bad parts. It is a sampling plan: for a given lot size and inspection level it fixes how many units get measured and how many defects force a reject. The reference standard is ISO 2859-1 (ANSI/ASQ Z1.4); China's GB/T 2828.1-2012 is the national adoption of the 1999 edition, so do not let a report cite one standard and quote tables from the other.

Lot size (pieces)Level II sampleAQL 1.0 accept / reject (major)AQL 4.0 accept / reject (minor)
151–280321 / 23 / 4
501–1,200802 / 35 / 6
3,201–10,0002005 / 610 / 11
10,001–35,00050010 / 1121 / 22
35,001–150,00080014 / 1521 / 22

General Inspection Level II is the default. Level I is used for low-risk parts when inspection budget is tight; Level III when a supplier has a history or a part is safety-related. Choose the level before the visit — changing it after seeing the result invalidates the plan.

Read sample size and accept/reject numbers as one package. A sample of 80 with 2/3 is not "80 parts checked, three defects allowed": find three major defects in that sample and the lot fails.

Classify Defects Before Production Starts

The whole AQL system depends on a decision made before the parts exist. Defect classes are an engineering decision, not an inspection decision, and they belong in the purchase order.

ClassDefinitionAuto parts exampleWorking AQL
CriticalSafety, regulatory, or total function failureWrong friction material on a brake pad; cracked steering knuckle; sensor with no output0 — one unit fails the lot
MajorFails in assembly or materially departs from specMounting hole out of position; thread will not engage; coating below spec1.0–1.5
MinorCosmetic or packaging, function unaffectedLight scratch on a non-visible face; dented outer carton4.0

Vague classes produce vague reports. "Minor burrs acceptable" becomes a negotiation at the inspection table. "Burr under 0.1 mm on machined edges, judged against the golden sample photo" is inspectable. Decide the counting unit too: one bracket with three scratches and a loose fastener is one nonconforming unit or four nonconformities, and the plan has to say which.

Safety parts are the exception to every number above. Brake, steering and suspension components get AQL 0 on critical defects, which in practice means the inspector is not sampling for those characteristics — the lot fails on the first one found.

What Gets Measured, by Category

A generic checklist wastes the visit. This is what a competent inspector does with each family.

Part familyPriority checksInstruments
Brake pads, discs, calipersFriction material composition, disc thickness and runout (commonly held to 0.02 mm), backing plate flatness, caliper bore diameter, ECE R90 documentation for EU-bound goodsXRF analyser, micrometer, dial indicator, roughness tester
Control arms, ball joints, tie rodsMounting hole alignment, ball joint torque range, bush hardness, weld integrityCMM, torque wrench, Shore A durometer
Engine sensors and coilsConnector pin-out against the OE reference, signal output across range, harness length, weather seal integrityMultimeter, oscilloscope, pin-out diagram
Filters (oil, air, fuel, cabin)Media quality and fold count, gasket dimensions, bypass valve spring tension, anti-drainback valve functionCaliper, fold counter, spring tester
Rubber and sealing partsHardness, compression set, dimensional fit, absence of flashShore durometer, caliper

Every measurement needs a reference: the approved drawing, the golden sample, or the OE part number with its stated tolerance. Without one the inspector judges by impression and the report carries no weight in a dispute.

Two documents are worth requesting at the same time because they are cheap to produce and hard to fake later: the material certificate (mill certificate or compound batch record) and the calibration certificate for the measuring equipment used in the factory's own final check.

The Written Protocol Decides the Dispute

One document, sent to both the agency and the factory before the visit, turns the inspection from an opinion into evidence. It should state:

  • The part numbers, quantities and lot identification being presented
  • The standard and edition governing sampling (ISO 2859-1, or GB/T 2828.1-2012 if that is what the contract cites), the inspection level, and the AQL per defect class
  • Product-specific defect definitions with examples — critical, major and minor, written for this part
  • The critical-to-function dimensions with tolerances and the instrument for each
  • Functional tests required, with pass criteria (torque range, pressure hold, signal range)
  • Packaging, labelling, barcode scannability and anti-corrosion requirements
  • Whether the golden sample or the drawing governs, and what happens when they disagree

Send it with the purchase order, not with the inspection booking. A protocol delivered two days before the visit is a protocol nobody has read.

Timing, and the Leverage You Have

Book the visit when production is complete and at least 80 percent of the cartons are packed — that is the industry convention, and it exists so the sample drawn represents the shipment rather than a display batch. Schedule it several days before the loading date so a failed result still leaves room to sort, rework or re-inspect.

A standard order is inspected in a day. Add time when the order spans many references or when functional testing is involved. The factory side prepares access to cartons, a measuring table, power, and the reference sample.

The economics are simple: the inspection happens before the balance is paid. A conforming report means the goods ship and the balance is released. A non-conforming report means the factory sorts, reworks or remakes, and a re-inspection confirms before loading. In between sits the negotiated discount, which is only available while the money is still yours.

For auto parts, the visit also produces something worth more than the pass/fail: dated photographs and measurements tied to a written requirement. That file is what you use when the same part number misbehaves in your market eight months later.

Container Loading Supervision: The Step Buyers Skip

Parts that pass inspection can still arrive damaged. Loading supervision is a separate, short visit that records carton count against the packing list, pallet and dunnage condition, stacking pattern, weight distribution, container condition before loading, and the seal number after closing. It also catches the substitution that PSI cannot: cartons loaded from a different lot than the ones sampled.

Ask for the seal number in the report and match it to the bill of lading. It costs a fraction of a full inspection day and it is the only evidence of what physically left.

When to Skip It, and When to Run It Twice

Skip a full PSI when the order is a repeat of a reference you have already shipped three times from the same plant, the value is below the cost of the visit, or the supplier has a documented in-process control system you have audited yourself. Replace it with a document review and a loading check.

Run it twice — DUPRO plus PSI, and sometimes a second PSI after rework — when the part is safety-related, when it is your first order from this plant, when the quotation came in materially below the others on the floor, or when the production window runs into the pre-holiday rush. A price that beat every other quote at the fair is usually explained by something, and inspection is how you find out what.

Never re-inspect on the same sample plan after a partial rework without agreeing which lots were sorted. Mixing sorted and unsorted cartons is the most common way a second inspection produces a meaningless pass.

Turning the Report into a Supplier Decision

One failed inspection tells you about a lot. Three tell you about a supplier. Keep a simple record: reference, lot, defect class counts, root cause given, and whether the fix held on the next order. Buyers who do this for a year end up with a shortlist that is based on measurements rather than on how pleasant the booth conversation was.

The other half is upstream. Agreeing the specification, the golden sample and the defect classes in writing before production is what makes the inspection fast and the argument short. Everything described here is cheaper than one rejected container, and almost all of it is decided in the week you place the order rather than the week the goods are ready.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much notice does a pre-shipment inspection need?

Book three to five working days ahead. The binding constraint is the 80 percent packed rule: the factory has to confirm that state before the inspector can draw a representative sample, so the date moves with production rather than with your calendar.

Who pays for the inspection?

Usually the buyer, because the buyer is the one who wants the evidence. What matters more than who pays is that the agency is instructed by you and reports to you, not to the factory that booked the room.

Is AQL 2.5 the right setting for auto parts?

It is the general-merchandise default and it is too loose for most of this category. Working practice for auto parts is AQL 0 on critical defects, 1.0–1.5 on major and 4.0 on minor, tightened further for brake, steering and suspension components.

What happens if the lot fails?

Three outcomes: the factory sorts or reworks and you re-inspect before loading; you accept with a documented price adjustment; or you reject and the order is remade. Which one is realistic depends on whether the balance is still unpaid — so the inspection must be before that payment, never after.

Can the factory's own final inspection replace a third-party visit?

It can complement it but not replace it. The factory's outgoing check may use a different standard or plan from yours; keep both records and do not merge the results unless the populations, methods and decision rules genuinely match. The value of an independent visit is that the sampling is random and the report belongs to you.

Does inspection cover regulatory compliance?

Only what you put in the protocol. EU-bound friction parts need ECE R90 documentation, and some markets require specific labelling or material declarations. Name the requirement in the protocol; inspectors verify documents that are listed, they do not guess which regulations apply to your destination.

title: Canton Fair 2026 Auto Parts Buyer's Guide: Phase 1 Dates, Registration & Sourcing Plan
description: Canton Fair 2026 auto parts buyer's guide: the 140th session runs October 15 – November 4 in Guangzhou, with auto parts in Phase 1 (October 15–19) at the Pazhou complex.
