title: Korean Auto Parts at Canton Fair: Sourcing Hyundai & Kia OE Parts from China
description: How to source Hyundai and Kia replacement parts from China: genuine vs OE-spec vs aftermarket, reading Korean part numbers, supplier clusters, category economics and red flags.
toc: Why Korean Parts Need a Different Method
Genuine, OE-Spec and Aftermarket: Three Tiers
How to Read a Hyundai / Kia Part Number
Where Korean-Parts Suppliers Actually Cluster
Which Categories Travel Well in a Container
Certifications That Mean Something, and Their Limits
Before the Container: The Five-Piece Sample Test
MOQ, Mixed Orders and Consolidation
What Actually Moves the Price
Red Flags Specific to Korean Programmes
Frequently Asked Questions
content:
Hyundai and Kia are the two largest vehicle brands in the Globalucar catalogue, and they are also the easiest to buy badly. Korean part numbers look interchangeable across model years, the aftermarket copies a genuine number down to the hyphen, and the difference between a part that fits and a part that fails in six months is usually a material certificate nobody asked for. This is the buyers’ guide to sourcing Hyundai and Kia parts out of China, written around what the OE number actually tells you and what it does not.

Why Korean Parts Need a Different Method

Sourcing Korean parts is not the same exercise as sourcing Toyota or Volkswagen parts, for three reasons that shape every decision below.

First, the part numbering is dense. A single model line generates hundreds of closely related numbers that differ by trim, market and production month, and two references one digit apart can be genuinely different parts. Second, the aftermarket copies the numbers. A box printed with a Hyundai-format reference tells you nothing about who made the part inside it. Third, genuine supply is controlled: factory parts for current models move through the manufacturer's own distribution, so what an independent Chinese exporter can legitimately offer is replacement parts built to the OE specification, not dealer-boxed genuine stock.

None of this makes Korean parts a bad category — it is one of the highest-volume replacement segments in Africa, the Middle East, Latin America and Central Asia, and Chinese supply is deep. It means the verification has to happen on the number and the material, not on the conversation. Our supplier verification process covers the company; this article covers the catalogue.

Genuine, OE-Spec and Aftermarket: Three Tiers

Most disputes in this category start with a buyer and a supplier using the same word for different things. Fix the vocabulary in the purchase order.

TierWhat it isPackaging and markingWhat you can realistically buy in China
Genuine (OE service part)Made by or for the vehicle manufacturer and distributed through its own channelBranded box, manufacturer label, country-of-origin marking, traceable lot codeRarely available from independent exporters at scale; treat any large offer with caution
OE-spec / OESMade by a supplier that produces for the OE line, or to the same drawing and material spec, sold without the vehicle brandNeutral or private-label box, part number traceable to the makerThe realistic target for a serious programme
AftermarketBuilt to fit and function, not necessarily to the OE material or toleranceSupplier's own brand, generic or buyer's private labelWidely available, quality spread is wide, inspection decides

Ask the supplier to state the tier in writing on the quotation, per line. "Genuine" in an email and "genuine" on an invoice are different claims, and only the second one is useful if you have to make it stick.

How to Read a Hyundai / Kia Part Number

Korean references follow a consistent shape: five digits, a hyphen, then a short alphanumeric suffix. The first block identifies the part group; the suffix carries the variant — side, trim, engine, market or revision.

ReferenceFamilyWhat the suffix usually varies by
04465-xxxxxDisc brake pad setEngine size, market, pad compound revision
58101-xxxxx / 58110-xxxxxBrake caliper (left / right)Side, brake package, model year
52810-xxxxxHub / axle seal and bearing groupDriveline, ABS or non-ABS
27501-xxxxxIgnition cable setEngine code
86350-xxxxxFront grilleTrim level, camera or sensor provision
92101-xxxxx / 92102-xxxxxHeadlamp (left / right)Side, halogen or LED, market

These patterns are indicative and must be verified against the specific VIN before ordering. The reliable method is: take the number off the part that is coming off the vehicle, confirm it against the catalogue for that VIN and production date, and only then ask for a quotation. Ordering from an application list alone is how containers of near-correct parts get shipped.

Two traps follow from this. A "replacement for" number is a cross-reference, not an equivalence claim — ask which dimensions and materials are held to the OE drawing and which are not. And a number shared across model years does not mean the parts are shared: a pad set may carry one reference across four years while the backing plate or compound changed twice.

Where Korean-Parts Suppliers Actually Cluster

China's Korean-parts trade is regional, and knowing the map saves a day at the fair.

  • Guangzhou (Baiyun district and the parts markets around it) — the densest cluster of Hyundai and Kia specialists, heavy on chassis, brake, suspension, engine and electrical parts, with export consolidation through Nansha and Shenzhen. Most Canton Fair exhibitors in this category are based here.
  • Yiwu — strong on lamps, body parts, filters and engines, priced for high-volume container buyers in Africa and the Middle East.
  • Northern ports (Beijing traders shipping through Tianjin) — long-standing specialists in engine, brake, suspension, chassis and electrical systems for Hyundai and Kia, typically with their own Korean-market links.
  • Shandong — manufacturing base for rubber, seals, filters and some chassis parts, geographically close to Korea and often the plant behind a Guangzhou trader's catalogue.

The practical question is not where the office is but where the parts are made. A Guangzhou trader quoting a Shandong plant's output can be a perfectly good supplier — but ask which plant, and whether you can inspect there. Combine this with the hall-by-hall walk-through if you are still on the floor.

Which Categories Travel Well in a Container

Freight economics decide the mix more than unit price does. A cheap bulky part can cost more to ship than it is worth; a small dense part can carry an entire container's margin.

CategoryFreight profileDemand patternInspection focus
Brake pads and shoesDense, ships wellFastest-turning wear item in most marketsCompound and friction coefficient, backing plate flatness, ECE R90 where required
Filters (oil, air, fuel, cabin)Bulky, low unit valueHigh volume, service-interval drivenMedia fold count, gasket fit, bypass and anti-drainback valves
Suspension and steeringHeavy, moderate volumeSteady, road-condition drivenHole alignment, ball joint torque, bush hardness, weld quality
Lamps and body partsBulky, damage-proneAccident and replacement drivenFitment, lens clarity, connector match, packaging protection
Sensors and electricalSmall, high unit valueGrowing with vehicle agePin-out, signal output, sealing — functional test, not just visual
Rubber, seals and mountsLight, cheap to shipHigh-margin fillerHardness, compression set, material batch record

A first container usually works best as one dense anchor category — brake pads or suspension — plus light, high-margin fillers. Starting with a bulky low-value category is how a first shipment loses money while every line looks profitable.

Certifications That Mean Something, and Their Limits

Three marks come up repeatedly in this category. Know what each one covers.

  • IATF 16949 — the automotive quality-management standard. It says the plant runs a documented system; it says nothing about whether the specific part you are buying is made on that line. Verify the certificate number, scope and validity in the issuing body's database rather than accepting a scan.
  • ECE R90 — required for replacement brake pads and linings sold into markets applying the regulation. It governs friction performance within a tolerance band around the OE part, not overall quality. Ask for the test report, not the logo.
  • ECE R13 / R10 / R118 — braking, electromagnetic compatibility and flammability respectively, relevant by destination and part type rather than universally.

The gap in all three is the same: they certify a process or a tested sample, not your lot. That is what the pre-shipment inspection and the material certificate are for.

Before the Container: The Five-Piece Sample Test

Samples are cheap; containers are not. Order five pieces of each critical reference — not one — and put them through this sequence before you commit volume.

  1. Fit it. On the actual vehicle or a known-good assembly. A sample that fits one trim and not the neighbouring one is telling you the cross-reference is incomplete.
  2. Measure it. Calipers on the critical-to-function dimensions against the drawing or an OE part. Photograph the readings.
  3. Weigh it. Weight is a fast proxy for material. A control arm or pad backing plate noticeably lighter than the reference is a specification change you were not told about.
  4. Stress the packaging. Drop the box, leave it in humidity overnight, scan the barcode. Packaging defects are the most common cause of complaints that have nothing to do with the part.
  5. Keep one sealed. The retained sample is your reference for the pre-shipment inspection and for any later dispute about what was agreed.

Ask for the material certificate with the samples, not with the shipment. If a supplier cannot produce a compound or mill certificate for a brake or suspension part at sample stage, they will not produce one later.

MOQ, Mixed Orders and Consolidation

Minimum quantities in this category are set by whether the part is stocked or has to be made, and by whether you want your own packaging.

SituationTypical minimumWhat to expect
Stocked catalogue reference, neutral boxLow — tens of pieces per referenceShips quickly; listings for common Korean seals and small parts show minimums from around ten pieces
Made-to-order or less common referenceHundreds of piecesProduction slot required; lead time typically measured in weeks
Buyer's own brand box, label or barcodeCommonly 500 pieces and upPrinting and packaging setup; worth it only on references you will reorder
Mixed-category containerNegotiated per referenceMost Korean-parts specialists will combine brake, chassis, filtration and electrical lines into one consolidation

The consolidation question is where a Guangzhou-based partner earns its keep: picking ten references across five factories into one container, with one inspection and one set of export documents. Ask who owns the consolidation — if the answer is "the factory", you are dependent on their relationships rather than on your own.

What Actually Moves the Price

On Korean references the spread between a first quotation and a settled one comes from five places, in descending order of impact: order quantity on the reference, packaging specification, material grade, payment terms, and freight terms. The material grade is the one to watch. A pad set quoted well below the others usually differs in compound or in backing plate thickness, and the difference will not show up in a photograph.

Put the specification into the proforma invoice — compound, dimensions, packaging, and the retained sample reference — and the price discussion becomes a comparison instead of an argument. Our price negotiation guide covers the mechanics of that conversation.

Red Flags Specific to Korean Programmes

  • "Genuine" at aftermarket prices. Large volumes of boxed genuine parts for current models are not available through independent exporters. Verify before you pay for the claim.
  • A catalogue that covers every brand equally. Depth in Hyundai and Kia with supporting breadth is normal. Equal depth in twelve marques usually means a trading desk, not a programme.
  • No material certificate for friction, suspension or load-bearing parts. This is the single most common gap and the one most worth walking away over.
  • Samples that are visibly better than the quotation. Ask whether the sample came from the production line or from a display stock.
  • Reluctance to name the plant. If inspection cannot be arranged at the manufacturing site, the supplier is selling you a relationship, not a supply chain.
  • One number for every model year. Korean references change by trim and production date; a supplier who never asks for the VIN is guessing.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I buy genuine Hyundai and Kia parts from China?

Genuine service parts for current models move through the vehicle manufacturer's own distribution, so large independent supplies are unusual and should be verified carefully. What Chinese exporters supply at scale is OE-specification and aftermarket parts, which is the right target for most export programmes.

How do I confirm a part number fits a specific vehicle?

Verify against the VIN and production date rather than the model name. Take the number from the part being replaced, check it in the catalogue for that VIN, and treat any cross-reference as a claim to be confirmed, not an equivalence.

What minimum order should I expect on Korean references?

Stocked catalogue parts can start in the tens of pieces per reference. Made-to-order parts run into the hundreds, and buyer-branded packaging commonly starts around 500 pieces. The minimum is per reference, so mixed containers are negotiated line by line.

Which certification matters most?

IATF 16949 for the plant's quality system, and ECE R90 with a test report for friction parts going to markets that apply it. Neither certifies your lot — that is what material certificates and pre-shipment inspection are for.

Is it better to buy from a factory or a Guangzhou trader?

A factory gives you control over specification and inspection; a trader gives you consolidation across references. Many buyers work with a specialist that does both, provided the plant is named and open to inspection.

Which categories should a first container start with?

One dense anchor with fast turnover — brake pads or suspension — plus light, high-margin fillers such as rubber mounts and filters. Avoid opening with bulky low-value lines; the freight eats the margin before the parts sell.

title: Importing Cars into South Africa in 2026: The RHD Rule, the Duty Stack, and Why Parts Clear Faster
description: South Africa bans used-car imports for resale, requires factory right-hand drive, and stacks 25% duty, ad valorem excise and 15% VAT. Full 2026 cost model.
toc: Why South Africa Is Not a Normal African Import Market
Gate One: Right-Hand Drive, Before Any Conversation About Price
Gate Two: The Duty Stack, Layer by Layer
Gate Two, Continued: A Landed-Cost Model You Can Reuse
Gate Three: Used Vehicles, Where the Permit Is the Entire Game
The NRCS Letter of Authority, and How It Fails
Electric and Hybrid: No Import Discount, Despite the Headlines
Durban, the SADC Corridor, and Why There Is No Left-Hand-Drive Loophole
What South Africa Actually Buys From China: Parts
A Pre-Shipment Checklist for South Africa
Frequently Asked Questions
content:
South Africa is the one large African market where price is the last question, not the first. A left-hand-drive car cannot be registered there at all, a used car usually cannot be imported at all, and a new car that clears both gates still carries a tax load of roughly 55–90% of its FOB value. This guide works through the three gates in order, models a landed cost band by band, and explains why auto parts reach South African buyers far more easily than complete vehicles do.

Why South Africa Is Not a Normal African Import Market

Most African markets that Chinese exporters serve are open by default: no local assembly to protect, no right-hand-drive requirement, and duty structures a broker can work with. South Africa is the opposite. It has a full domestic vehicle industry — Toyota, Volkswagen, Ford, Nissan, Isuzu, Mercedes-Benz and BMW all assemble there under the Automotive Production and Development Programme — and the tariff schedule is written to keep imports at a deliberate price disadvantage.

The headline numbers from the industry association NAAMSA are 25% import duty on light vehicles and 20% on original equipment components, with a preferential 18% for European-origin vehicles under the SADC–EU arrangement. Layered on top are an ad valorem excise duty that rises with price, VAT at 15%, a CO2 emissions levy on new vehicles, and R2,000–R10,000 of clearing and inspection cost per unit.

A Chinese brand can compete here, and several do profitably, but only after committing to factory right-hand-drive production and a local homologation file. Sending a left-hand-drive unit to Durban because the price looked good on paper is the most common expensive mistake in this trade.

Gate One: Right-Hand Drive, Before Any Conversation About Price

South Africa drives on the left. Registration requires a right-hand-drive vehicle, and the National Regulator for Compulsory Specifications (NRCS) will not issue a Letter of Authority for a converted unit. The only surviving exception is narrow: vehicles already registered in South Africa before the current rules took effect, in practice cars first registered around 2000 or earlier.

This is not a problem a workshop can solve. Conversion changes the firewall, the steering rack, the pedal box, the wiring loom and the crash structure, and no registration authority will accept the result on a vehicle imported after the cut-off. A left-hand-drive unit that lands in Durban is, functionally, a parts donor.

So the first question about any model is not the FOB price but whether the factory builds it in right-hand drive for export and whether that build is approved for South African registration. The Chinese brands selling in volume — Chery with Omoda and Jaecoo, GWM's Haval range, BYD, LDV and Maxus, JAC, BAIC — did that work at factory level before shipping a single unit. Most of the SUV and EV ranges that move well in the Gulf and West Africa are left-hand drive only.

Ask any sourcing channel for the right-hand-drive confirmation in writing, with the model code. Verbal assurance is worth nothing here, because the cost of being wrong is a container of unsellable metal on a Durban quay.

Gate Two: The Duty Stack, Layer by Layer

South African customs value is FOB, not CIF, so ocean freight is excluded from the duty base. That is the one piece of good news in the calculation. Everything else compounds.

LayerCharged onRateWhat it means in practice
Customs dutyFOB customs value25% (18% EU/UK origin, 0% SADC origin)Charged first, and it becomes part of the VAT base
Ad valorem exciseExcise value: retail price excluding VAT, less 20%(0.00003 × excise value) − 0.75%, capped at 30%Progressive. Negligible on a budget car, punitive on a luxury one
VATFOB × 1.10, plus duty, plus ad valorem15%The 10% uplift means VAT is never simply 15% of the invoice
CO2 emissions levyGrams of CO2 per kilometre, new vehicles onlyR146/g at the 2024 rate, adjusted annuallySmall on a 120 g/km car, material on a large SUV or pickup
Compliance and clearingPer unitNRCS Letter of Authority R300–R1,800, plus agent feesFixed cost, but it doubles on a unit that needs re-inspection

The ad valorem formula is the part most buyers get wrong, because it is keyed to retail price rather than to what you paid. Work the excise value from the price the car will actually sell for, subtract 20%, apply the formula, cap at 30%. Below roughly R1.0 million of excise value the rate is still climbing; above it the cap holds and the percentage stops rising even as the rand amount keeps growing.

Gate Two, Continued: A Landed-Cost Model You Can Reuse

Here is the arithmetic on four price bands, using a retail equivalent of 1.9 times FOB (a workable assumption for an imported unit with local margin), R38,000 of freight and insurance, R6,000 of clearing and R1,800 for the Letter of Authority. Every figure is in rand and every assumption is stated, so you can substitute your own.

LineFOB R180,000FOB R220,000FOB R350,000FOB R800,000
Customs duty at 25%R45,000R55,000R87,500R200,000
Ad valorem rate applied6.45%8.02%13.13%30.00% (capped)
Ad valorem exciseR15,480R23,418R60,732R317,217
VAT at 15% on the added tax valueR38,772R48,063R79,985R209,583
Total taxR99,252R126,481R228,217R726,800
Tax as a share of FOB55.1%57.5%65.2%90.8%
Landed cost at the portR325,052R392,281R624,017R1,572,600

Read the last two rows together. The tax take is not flat: it climbs from about 55% on a budget unit to about 91% on a high-value one, because ad valorem is progressive and because VAT is charged on the duty and the excise as well as on the car. A model that looks competitive at FOB R180,000 is a different commercial proposition at FOB R800,000, and a plan built on the cheap end of a range will not survive being applied to the expensive end. It is also why luxury Chinese EVs, the segment most exporters are excited about, are the hardest to land profitably here.

Gate Three: Used Vehicles, Where the Permit Is the Entire Game

South Africa restricts used-vehicle imports to protect local assembly, and the restriction is close to absolute. The International Trade Administration Commission (ITAC) issues permits only within defined categories, and there is no general permit for importing a used car to resell. Every permit carries an undertaking not to sell or dispose of the vehicle for two years, which closes the resale route by design.

CategoryApplicationKey conditionResale restriction
Returning South African residentForm IE462Six months or more abroad, vehicle registered in the applicant's name for that periodTwo-year undertaking, and the car may not ship before the owner returns
Immigrant with permanent residenceForm IE462Permanent residence certificate plus foreign registration documentTwo-year undertaking
Inherited vehicleForm IE462Deceased estate documentationTwo-year undertaking
Vintage or collector vehicleForm IE462Generally 40 years or older, or a recognised collector's itemTwo-year undertaking
Disability-adapted vehicleForm IE463Specially designed or adapted for a disabled South African nationalTwo-year undertaking
Racing or track vehicleForm IE462Not for use on public roadsTwo-year undertaking

For qualifying returning residents and immigrants there is a duty rebate on one vehicle per family on a permanent change of residence, claimed on form DA304A at the border. The conditions are that the vehicle was owned and used for at least twelve months before departure and is not sold within twenty months of entry. That rebate is the difference between a sensible move and a bad one.

Anything outside these categories should be treated as unimportable, whatever a broker says. Permits are tied to a named applicant and a named vehicle, ITAC and SARS validate against each other, and an unpermitted unit is not registrable, not insurable and liable to seizure. If you are buying used stock from China for African markets, the West and East African corridors are where it belongs; South Africa is not.

The NRCS Letter of Authority, and How It Fails

Every imported vehicle needs a Letter of Authority from the NRCS before it can be registered or licensed, whether new, used, inherited, donated or brought in by a returning resident. The application is made on form LA01 with a fee of about R300 to R1,800 depending on vehicle type and age, submitted by email and routed by the first letter of the applicant's surname or company name.

NRCS processing is often quoted at around five working days, but the honest end-to-end number is four to eight weeks once test reports and model-level compliance evidence are counted. Manufacturers hold that file already; a first-time importer of a model never registered in South Africa does not.

The failure modes are predictable. A model with no South African compliance history needs evidence the importer cannot produce quickly. A VIN or engine number that does not match the invoice stops the file. A left-hand-drive unit fails on the face of it, and a vehicle modified after manufacture can fail because the modification sits outside the original approval. Apply before booking freight, not after the vessel sails; storage at the terminal runs at hundreds of rand a day.

Electric and Hybrid: No Import Discount, Despite the Headlines

South Africa taxes electric vehicles at the same 25% duty as petrol and diesel cars. The much-quoted incentive introduced from 1 March 2026 — a 150% capital-investment allowance under Section 12X of the Income Tax Act — is a production-side deduction for manufacturers building vehicles inside South Africa. It is not an import rebate, and it does nothing for a container arriving from Guangzhou.

Worse for the EV case, ad valorem is keyed to price and electric drivetrains push price up. A high-value electric SUV can carry the 30% cap plus 25% duty plus 15% VAT, which is how the tax take reaches the 90% band above. Hybrids sit in the same 25% customs line as other passenger cars. The structure has been criticised domestically for exactly this reason, and a submission to the 2026 Budget argued for alignment between the electric and combustion rates; it was not actioned in February.

One related change worth knowing: from 1 June 2026, foreign-registered vehicles entering South Africa temporarily must be declared and carry a Temporary Import Permit. It targets travellers rather than commercial importers, but it signals that border enforcement is tightening.

Durban, the SADC Corridor, and Why There Is No Left-Hand-Drive Loophole

Durban is the busiest vehicle port in sub-Saharan Africa, and Transnet's car terminals at Durban, East London and Gqeberha handled 792,574 vehicles in the eleven months to mid-February 2026 — imports, exports and transhipments combined. It is also the in-bond gateway for the region, which leads to a question exporters ask constantly: can a left-hand-drive unit clear in Durban and be sold across the border instead?

Usually no. South Africa's immediate partners — Zimbabwe, Zambia, Botswana, Lesotho, Eswatini, Malawi and Mozambique — all drive on the left, and Namibia, also left-hand traffic, is served through Walvis Bay. The right-hand-drive requirement covers the whole southern corridor, not just South Africa. The genuine left-hand-drive markets sit further north: Nigeria, Ghana, Ethiopia, Angola and the Democratic Republic of Congo, reached through Lagos, Mombasa, Dar es Salaam or Matadi.

What Durban does offer is transit: an in-bond movement under a SAD500 declaration to a named SADC buyer, with the vehicle never entering South African use. That is a legitimate structure for right-hand-drive stock bound for Harare or Lusaka, and worth using when volume justifies the bond.

What South Africa Actually Buys From China: Parts

Step back from the vehicle question and the commercial picture reverses. South Africa's car parc is dominated by models assembled locally — the Toyota Hilux, Volkswagen Polo Vivo, Ford Ranger and Isuzu D-Max among them — which means a large, mature, price-sensitive aftermarket with no right-hand-drive complication, no ITAC permit and no Letter of Authority. Import duty on components sits between 0% and 20% depending on the tariff line, and clearance is measured in days rather than months.

That is where friction is lowest for a Chinese-sourced range, and it is why our own South African conversations tend to end up in brake, cooling, suspension and engine parts rather than complete vehicles. A workshop in Johannesburg replacing pads and rotors on a Hilux does not care where the box came from; it cares that the reference is right, the bedding-in behaviour is predictable and the next container arrives on schedule. Our duty cheat sheet for African and Middle Eastern markets covers the component side of the tariff schedule line by line.

Two practical notes for anyone building a parts programme here. Quote OEM-grade quality rather than brand-name packaging, because the compliance risk of shipping product in another manufacturer's livery is not worth the margin. And work from OE numbers rather than model names, because the same Hilux generation carries different references across assembly plants. Our parts finder and the OE number index exist so a buyer can confirm the reference before the order, not after.

A Pre-Shipment Checklist for South Africa

If you are serious about a South African programme, run these eight checks in order. Each one has killed deals that looked fine at the quotation stage.

  1. Confirm factory right-hand drive in writing, with the model code and the OEM's export-market list.
  2. Check the model's South African compliance history before quoting. No history means a compliance file you may not be able to build.
  3. Model ad valorem from retail equivalent, not from FOB, and apply the 30% cap.
  4. Get the ITAC position in writing if the unit is used. Not one of the six categories means stop.
  5. Apply for the Letter of Authority early and budget four to eight weeks, not five days.
  6. Appoint a SARS-registered clearing agent before booking freight, and confirm terminal storage tariffs.
  7. Inspect and photograph before loading, including the VIN plate and odometer; pre-shipment evidence is what settles damage claims.
  8. Ask for the landed number, not the FOB number. A supplier who cannot produce the tax stack has not done this before.

Tell us the model and the destination, and we will tell you which gate it fails. For right-hand-drive models with an existing South African compliance history we quote factory availability and FOB Nansha pricing; for everything else we will say so plainly rather than book a container that cannot be registered. Parts enquiries — brake, cooling, suspension, engine, electrical — are quoted FOB Guangzhou within 48 hours from an OE list. Send the list through the enquiry form or by WhatsApp on +86 133-0240-8528.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I import a used car into South Africa to resell?
No. ITAC permits are issued only for returning residents, immigrants with permanent residence, inherited vehicles, vintage or collector vehicles, disability-adapted vehicles and racing cars, and every permit carries a two-year no-resale undertaking. There is no permit category for commercial resale.

How much does it cost to import a car into South Africa in 2026?
Budget 55% of FOB on a cheap unit and up to 90% on an expensive one, made up of 25% customs duty, ad valorem excise on a sliding scale capped at 30%, and 15% VAT charged on the added tax value. On an FOB of R220,000 that is roughly R126,000 in tax before freight and clearing.

Is left-hand drive allowed in South Africa?
Not for vehicles imported now. Registration requires right-hand drive and the NRCS will not issue a Letter of Authority for a converted unit. The only practical exception is vehicles already registered in South Africa before the current rules, in practice around 2000 or earlier.

Do I need an ITAC permit for a new car?
No. New vehicles do not require an ITAC import permit. They do require an NRCS Letter of Authority, a customs declaration through a clearing agent, and payment of duty, ad valorem excise and VAT.

Can I ship a left-hand-drive car through Durban to Zimbabwe or Zambia?
Not usefully. Both countries drive on the left and require right-hand drive, as do Botswana, Lesotho, Eswatini, Malawi and Mozambique. Durban's in-bond transit works for right-hand-drive stock moving to those markets; it does not create a route for left-hand-drive vehicles.

How long does an NRCS Letter of Authority take?
NRCS processing is often quoted at about five working days once a complete file is lodged, but the realistic end-to-end timeline is four to eight weeks when test reports and model-level evidence have to be assembled. The fee is R300 to R1,800. Apply before booking freight.

Quick Answer: Iran's auto parts aftermarket is structurally undersupplied because roughly five to seven million aging Toyota Corolla, RAV4, Hyundai Elantra and Kia Rio/Sportage vehicles are still in service with no official Toyota or Hyundai/Kia distribution behind them. Six categories dominate: brake pads and rotors, cooling and air-conditioning, ignition and engine management, suspension top mounts and bushings, oxygen and ABS sensors, and oil/air/fuel/cabin filters. Wholesale pricing out of Guangzhou for these categories runs from roughly USD 3 for a cabin filter to USD 180 for a hybrid inverter cooling plate, with container economics working at 4,000 to 12,000 pieces per 40HQ depending on the part type. The compliance caveat is the same as for the vehicle lane: buyers must verify their own sanctions and import rules before booking.

If you run a wholesale auto-parts desk in Guangzhou, the most important structural fact about the Iranian aftermarket in 2026 is that it is not a developing market — it is a recovering market that lost its official supply line in 2018 and never got it back. The Toyota, Hyundai and Kia vehicles on Iranian roads are mostly between five and fifteen years old. The OEM dealer network that would have supplied replacement parts for those vehicles disappeared under sanctions. What replaced it is a layered aftermarket — local Iranian parts makers producing to reverse-engineered OE specs, used parts stripped from end-of-life vehicles in neighbouring jurisdictions, and a steadily growing import flow out of Chinese ports that is now the marginal source for several high-velocity part categories. The composition of that import flow is what this guide is about.

1. Iran's Fleet Reality: Millions of Aging Japanese and Korean Cars with No Official Supply Line

To understand the parts market, you have to understand the fleet. Iran's passenger vehicle parc is roughly 14 to 16 million units, of which an estimated 35 to 45 per cent is the Toyota Corolla family (sedan, Cross, older Sprinter), the first-generation Toyota RAV4, the Kia Rio and Pride, the Hyundai Elantra (XD, MD, AD generations), the Hyundai Sonata (EF, YF, LF), and a smaller but persistent share of the Kia Sportage. Almost all of these vehicles were either officially imported in the 2005 to 2017 window, or were reassembled from CKD kits through IKCO and SAIPA lines. The 2018 sanctions did not remove these vehicles from the road. They removed the official Toyota, Hyundai and Kia parts pipeline that would have supported them. What remains is the aftermarket.

The mechanics of the gap matter. A 2014 Toyota Corolla owner in Tehran today cannot order a genuine Toyota cabin air filter through the official Toyota Iran dealer network, because the official dealer network no longer exists in the form that would service that order. The owner instead buys either an aftermarket filter from a Tehran-area workshop that sources through the Jafari Bazaar parts district, a reverse-engineered equivalent from a local Iranian manufacturer, or — increasingly — an imported aftermarket filter from a wholesale distributor in Guangzhou, Dubai, or Istanbul who is buying the part at container scale. The third of these three flows is the one the global wholesale desk in 2026 should be pricing for, because it is the one with the most stable documentary profile and the lowest per-unit landed cost.

2. Why Iranian Workshops Prefer Japanese Cars: Parts Availability and Repair Simplicity

The argument is not sentimental. It is mechanical. Iranian workshops are calibrated to Japanese cars because three decades of accumulated practice have made the typical 2007 Corolla or 2012 Elantra faster to diagnose and faster to repair than a 2023 CKD Chery Tiggo 7. The wire harness layout is known, the diagnostic protocols are standard, the bolt patterns are standard, and the parts inventory is deep. A workshop that can turn around a Toyota brake job in two hours will need four hours and a proprietary diagnostic tool for a comparable job on a Chinese CKD. That productivity gap is what keeps Japanese cars dominant in the Iranian workshop queue, and it is what gives the Japanese parts aftermarket its structural depth.

For a wholesale distributor, the implication is direct. A Toyota or Hyundai/Kia aftermarket part shipped to Iran is being shipped into a market that already knows how to install it, knows what a good one looks like, and knows what a bad one looks like. The risk of "the part doesn't fit" is materially lower than it is for a less-established nameplate. The risk of "the part arrives broken" is the same as for any other lane and is managed through pre-shipment inspection rather than through market education.

3. The Six Highest-Demand Part Categories for the Iranian Aftermarket

Six categories account for the bulk of the volume of the import lane into the Iranian aftermarket. Each has its own unit economics, its own OE reference patterns, and its own certification burden.

Brake pads and rotors. Brake pads are a 3,000 to 8,000 km wear item on Tehran traffic, and the Iranian taxi fleet alone consumes them at industrial scale. OE references for the Corolla 1.8L run across the D1217 / D1224 pad families and the 43512-series rotor family. RAV4 2.0L and 2.5L share a rotor generation that is widely cross-referenced. Rotor diameter, pad friction grade (ceramic, semi-metallic, low-metallic NAO) and ECE R90 certification for the European-style destination flows all matter. Pad pricing out of Guangzhou FOB runs from roughly USD 6 to USD 18 per axle set depending on grade; rotors run from USD 18 to USD 55 per piece depending on diameter and coating (plain, drilled, slotted, painted).

Cooling and air-conditioning. Cooling is the second-highest volume category, and it is the one that interacts most directly with the local environmental stress. Tehran summer ambient temperatures run above 40°C for sustained periods, which shortens radiator hose life, condenser life, and AC compressor life well below the OEM design envelope. Radiators, condensers, electric cooling fans, expansion tanks, and AC compressors are all on the high-velocity list. Pricing out of Guangzhou for the Toyota Corolla 1.8L aluminium radiator is roughly USD 38-65 per piece, with a 20-piece carton. Condensers run USD 22-40 per piece. AC compressors for the RAV4 hybrid variants run USD 160-220 per piece. The hybrid-specific cooling plate (the plate that sits under the inverter) is its own category and prices higher than the conventional radiator at roughly USD 140-180 per piece.

Ignition and engine management. Pencil coils, spark plugs, ignition leads, the throttle body, and the engine control unit are the engine-management layer. For the Toyota 1.8L and 2.0L four-cylinder the pencil-coil pricing is roughly USD 8-14 per piece at the FOB level, with 50-piece cartons. The aftermarket plug pricing for iridium and platinum grades runs USD 1.8-3.5 per piece at the FOB level. Throttle bodies for the Corolla 1.8L run USD 45-80 per piece. ECU pricing is significantly higher and more variable.

Suspension top mounts, bushings, and shock absorbers. Tehran's road surface is hard on rubber and polyurethane parts. Top mounts, control arm bushings, and the front strut cartridges all see accelerated wear. Top mount pricing for the Corolla and Elantra is roughly USD 5-12 per piece at the FOB level. Shock absorbers (front struts as a complete cartridge) run USD 22-55 per piece depending on the brand tier. Bushings come in by the bag (typically 20 to 50 pieces per bag) at USD 0.4-1.2 per piece at the FOB level.

Oxygen, MAF, MAP, and ABS sensors. The sensor category is the one that is most exposed to quality variation, because a bad oxygen sensor does not look any different from a good one in the carton. The Iranian workshop layer is calibrated to know this and prices accordingly: the OE-equivalent oxygen sensor for a Corolla 1.8L runs USD 18-35 per piece at the FOB level, and the workshop will typically install two as a pair. The ABS wheel speed sensor runs USD 12-28 per piece. The MAF sensor for the Corolla and RAV4 runs USD 28-55 per piece. The MAP sensor is cheaper at USD 8-18 per piece.

Oil, air, fuel, and cabin filters. Filters are the volume backbone of the aftermarket import lane. A filter is light, cheap, and easy to ship, which is why this category works as a container-stuffer alongside higher-value parts. The pricing out of Guangzhou FOB for the four common filter types is roughly: oil filter USD 0.6-1.5 per piece (100 pieces per carton); air filter USD 1.2-2.8 per piece (50 pieces per carton); fuel filter USD 1.5-3.5 per piece (50 pieces per carton); cabin filter (the activated-carbon type that sells in Iran because of the dust load) USD 1.0-2.4 per piece (50 pieces per carton). The cabin filter is the most-velocity item on a per-container basis.

4. Toyota Corolla and RAV4: The Anchor Nameplates of Iran's Aftermarket

The Toyota Corolla and the Toyota RAV4 together account for the largest single block of the Iranian aftermarket import lane. The Corolla is the taxi-fleet backbone of every major Iranian city. The RAV4 (mostly the third-generation XA40) is the family SUV of choice for the Iranian upper-middle class and is also a strong second-hand rental fleet vehicle. Both nameplates have OE references that have been stable for two decades, which means an aftermarket part cross-referenced to a 2010 Corolla usually fits the 2017 Corolla and very often the 2020 Corolla as well. The reference density for these two nameplates is what makes them the most economical to import at scale.

5. Hyundai Elantra and Kia Sportage: The Korean Workhorses of Tehran's Taxi Fleet

The Korean side of the Iranian aftermarket is dominated by the Hyundai Elantra (XD, MD, AD generations) and the Kia Sportage, with a smaller but persistent share for the Kia Rio and the Hyundai Sonata. The Elantra in particular is the second-largest single nameplate in the Iranian taxi fleet after the Corolla, and the Elantra's parts pattern is the one a Korean parts desk in Guangzhou should be pricing for. The Kia Sportage is the Korean family SUV of choice in Iran and runs against the RAV4 on price positioning in the wholesale lane.

6. OE References and Cross-Compatibility: What to Verify Before Ordering

The single largest source of after-sales dispute in the cross-border parts lane is the cross-reference error. A distributor quotes an OE reference for a 2010 Corolla 1.8L radiator; the buyer's workshop receives it and finds that the hose connection is for a 2014 Corolla 1.6L. Both distributors and workshops are right from their own perspective, and the dispute is genuinely the result of incomplete cross-referencing. The fix is procedural, not commercial: every OE reference should be quoted with the engine code, the build year, the transmission type, and where relevant the regional market variant. The buyer's VIN gives you the four pieces of information; the seller's catalogue gives you the cross-reference. The cross-check is the buyer's responsibility before shipping.

7. Quality Grades and Certification: IATF 16949, ECE R90 and What Iranian Importers Actually Ask For

Two certifications dominate the conversation. IATF 16949 is the global quality management standard for automotive parts manufacture; a factory with IATF 16949 certification is operating under the same quality discipline as an OE factory, even if the parts it produces are aftermarket-grade rather than OE-genuine. ECE R90 is the European brake-component regulation, and is the relevant certification for brake pads and rotors exported to jurisdictions that follow the European vehicle regulation regime. The Iranian aftermarket accepts both grades, but the workshop layer prices accordingly: a brake pad with ECE R90 certification sells at a 30 to 50 per cent premium over an equivalent pad without it. The general rule for a wholesale distributor pricing the Iran-bound container is to stock a 60/40 mix: 60 per cent of the IATF 16949 aftermarket grade, 40 per cent of the IATF 16949 + ECE R90 grade. The workshop's "premium job" trade will absorb the latter.

8. FOB Guangzhou Price Ladder and Container Economics

The container economics for the Iranian aftermarket are favourable for the mixed-category container. A 40HQ running a mix of brake pads, rotors, filters, ignition coils and top mounts in the proportions above will hold roughly 4,000 to 12,000 pieces depending on which categories are weighted. The cabin filter is the densest item at roughly 6,000 pieces per 40HQ if loaded pallet-on-pallet. The brake rotor is the bulkiest at roughly 600 pieces per 40HQ. The pencil coil runs roughly 4,000 pieces per 40HQ. The AC compressor runs roughly 240 pieces per 40HQ. The hybrid inverter cooling plate is the bulkiest by weight at roughly 200 pieces per 40HQ.

For a wholesale buyer pricing the Iran-bound container in October 2026, the indicative per-container FOB Guangzhou value is roughly USD 38,000 to USD 95,000 depending on the mix. The Iranian-side landed cost (freight, insurance, Iranian customs duty, local inland transport) typically runs another 25 to 40 per cent on top, depending on the documentary structure. The per-piece margin available to the buyer ranges from 30 per cent on filters to 80 to 120 per cent on sensors and AC compressors. The whole category economics work because the volume is there and the workshop layer is calibrated to install the parts without service-cost surprises.

9. Shipping Routes and Payment Realities for Iran-Bound Parts

Two shipping routes run in parallel. The deep-water option goes from Nansha or Shanghai through the Strait of Hormuz to Bandar Abbas, with onward trucking to Tehran, Isfahan, Mashhad or Tabriz. The overland option goes by rail to a consolidation point in a neighbouring jurisdiction and then overland into Iran; the documentary profile is different and the transit time is longer. Both routes are well-established in 2026. The cross-border wholesale lane is not new, but the volume has grown materially in the last twelve months as Chinese-port supply has become the marginal source for several categories.

The payment reality is that the cross-border lane operates under the same documentary discipline as the vehicle lane, with a third-country finance and insurance structure typically used to manage sanctions reach. The buyer's sanctions verification is the buyer's responsibility, and the seller's role is to deliver the parts to the buyer's nominated port against the buyer's letter of credit or equivalent instrument. Buyers and importers must independently verify applicable sanctions, export-control and import regulations for their destination market and consult qualified trade-compliance counsel before any booking. That sentence is the same one on the vehicle guide for the same reason: in 2026 the documentary discipline is the deal.

10. Frequently Asked Questions

What is the size of the Iranian auto parts aftermarket today?

Iran's passenger parc is roughly 14 to 16 million units, of which 35 to 45 per cent is the Toyota Corolla family, the first-generation RAV4, the Hyundai Elantra, the Kia Rio/Pride, and the Hyundai Sonata. The official Toyota, Hyundai and Kia parts pipeline that would have supported these vehicles was effectively cut in 2018. What replaced it is a layered aftermarket — local Iranian manufacturers producing to reverse-engineered OE specifications, used parts stripped from end-of-life vehicles in the Gulf and Central Asia, and a steadily growing import flow out of Chinese ports. The import flow is the marginal source for several categories and is the lane a Chinese-port wholesale desk should be pricing for in 2026.

Which categories move the most volume into the Iranian aftermarket?

Six categories account for the bulk: brake pads and rotors, cooling and air-conditioning, ignition and engine management, suspension top mounts and bushings, oxygen and ABS sensors, and the four filter types (oil, air, fuel, cabin). Of these, filters are the highest-volume container stuffer at roughly 6,000 cabin filters per 40HQ. Brake pads and rotors are the highest-revenue per container for the workshop trade. AC compressors and inverter cooling plates are the highest-margin individual items.

Why is the Toyota Corolla the anchor nameplate for the Iranian aftermarket?

Two reasons. First, volume: the Corolla family is the largest single nameplate in the Iranian taxi fleet, with an estimated parc of 3.5 to 4.5 million units across the E140, E170 and E210 generations. Second, reference stability: the OE reference pattern for the Corolla 1.8L four-cylinder has been stable for two decades, which means an aftermarket part cross-referenced to a 2010 Corolla usually fits the 2017 and very often the 2020 Corolla as well. That reference density is what makes the Corolla the most economical nameplate to import at scale.

What is the IATF 16949 certification and does the Iranian market care about it?

IATF 16949 is the global quality management standard for automotive parts manufacture. A factory operating under IATF 16949 is subject to the same quality discipline as an OE factory, even if the parts it produces are aftermarket-grade rather than OE-genuine. The Iranian workshop layer prices for it. An IATF 16949 aftermarket part sells at a 20 to 40 per cent premium over an equivalent non-certified part. The general rule for a 40HQ container bound for Iran is 60 per cent IATF 16949 aftermarket grade and 40 per cent IATF 16949 + ECE R90 (for brake parts) grade.

How are OE references cross-referenced for an Iran-bound parts order?

Every OE reference should be quoted with the engine code, the build year, the transmission type, and the regional market variant. The buyer's VIN gives the four pieces of information; the seller's catalogue gives the cross-reference. The cross-check is the buyer's responsibility before shipping. The indicative OE references in this guide are starting points for that cross-check, not final answers — the same OE reference family covers multiple part positions on the same vehicle, and the wrong position will fit loosely and fail quickly.

What does a wholesale buyer need to verify before booking a container to Iran?

Three things, in this order. First, the buyer's own jurisdiction's sanctions rules, including any U.S. OFAC reach, any EU export-control rules, and any destination-country import licensing. Second, the documentary structure of the transaction — Incoterms 2020 terms, letter of credit or equivalent instrument, third-country finance and insurance if applicable. Third, the parts mix and the cross-references — engine code, build year, transmission type, regional variant. Globalucar will support the documentary and cross-reference side of the booking; the legal characterisation of the transaction is a matter for the buyer's own trade-compliance counsel.

Quick Answer: Demand for Japanese cars in Iran surged through 2026 because the country's fuel shortfall, currency collapse and aging fleet finally ran into Toyota's Middle East supply cuts. As Toyota trimmed production after Hormuz disruptions and Iranian importers waited two months for replacement stock, buyers turned to alternative sources — including Chinese ports, where RAV4 2026, Corolla 2026, Corolla Cross, Frontlander, Elantra, Sonata, K5 and Sportage are all currently available FOB. This guide walks through why Japan-built stock has become a hard currency in Iran again, what the 2026 import lists actually say, and how cross-border distributors price the eight high-demand nameplates for the Iranian market today.

If you sell wholesale vehicles out of Guangzhou, the question of the year from October 2025 onward is no longer "do you have Chery for Central Asia" — it is some version of "do you have Japanese badged stock for Iran". The shift did not come from a policy change in Tehran. It came from three pressures meeting in the same month: Iran's daily gasoline shortfall expanded to fourteen to fifteen million litres per day, the rial fell toward 1,810,000 IRR per dollar, and Toyota issued two Middle East production cuts in quick succession after Hormuz shipping disruptions. By August 2026 the Iranian vice president for energy optimisation, Esfahjani, was on national television saying publicly that locally-assembled Chinese cars were "unreasonably priced, with poor quality stability and high running cost", and that importing Japanese complete vehicles "would have given citizens a better driving experience and a lower total cost". The remark was a political venting point, not a market signal — but the demand underneath it is real, and it is now reshaping the wholesale lane that runs from Chinese ports to Bandar Abbas.

1. Why Iran Suddenly Cannot Stop Talking About Japanese Cars Again

The "Japan is better" line in Tehran is older than the current sanctions cycle, but it has come back with force in 2026 for three reasons that have nothing to do with sentiment and everything to do with operating reality. The first is the fuel math. Iran's daily gasoline consumption hit roughly 145 million litres at peak, while domestic refining capacity sits near 121 million litres. The shortfall, fourteen to fifteen million litres per day, is structural — Iran's maritime fuel import channel has been choked since 2018 and no replacement is on the horizon. The second is the rial. By late April 2026 the rial had fallen to 1,810,000 per dollar, and the twelve-month average inflation was already past fifty per cent. A car, in that environment, is no longer a discretionary purchase — it is the most liquid hard asset an Iranian family can hold. The third is the auto stock itself. Roughly five to seven million of the passenger vehicles on Iranian roads are second-generation Toyota Corollas, first-generation Kia Rio/Hyundai Elantra, and first-gen Toyota RAV4. Most are over ten years old, none are being replaced on schedule, and every workshop in Tehran keeps a permanent shelf of parts for them.

The vice president's remarks on 16 August 2026 were unusual only because they were made on a live broadcast rather than a closed cabinet meeting. The same calculation runs in every Iranian household that owns a car: which vehicle will still be cheap to run, easy to repair, and worth something on the second-hand market five years from now? Japanese cars answer that question today. Chinese cars, which briefly held a 19.7 per cent share of the Iranian passenger market in 2025, are losing that share in 2026 not because their engineering is poor but because the CKD-assembly quality inside Iran is inconsistent, the spare-part pipeline is fragile, and the residual values are being marked down by local dealers in anticipation of even more supply cuts.

2. The Iranian Car Market at a Glance: 1.08M Units, Two Local Giants, a Shrinking Chinese CKD Presence

Iran produced roughly 1.078 million passenger and light commercial vehicles in 2024 according to OICA, making it one of the largest single-country automotive markets in the Middle East after Turkey and Egypt. Roughly seventy per cent of that volume is split between two state-linked assemblers — Iran Khodro (IKCO) and SAIPA — whose product lines are mostly pre-2015 platforms that the sanctions have prevented them from refreshing. Chinese brands filled the gap between 2018 and 2025 by shipping complete knock-down kits into Iran for local assembly, peaking at 19.7 per cent market share in 2025, with Chery the largest single foreign brand by volume. That run peaked and then reversed. Geely terminated its CKD and SKD operations in Iran in January 2026, including the closure of its local sales network. The joint Changan-SAIPA assembly project was wound down over the same period. As of October 2026, only Chery maintains a meaningful local presence, and that presence is now asset-light — small-volume whole-vehicle imports plus spare-parts supply, not factory build.

The wholesale lane — the one in which distributors buy containers of vehicles from a Chinese port, document them at Bandar Abbas or a partner port, and on-sell to local dealer networks inside Iran — is the one that has grown the most in 2026. That is the lane this guide is written for.

3. Why Japanese Cars Fit Iran's Operating Reality: Fuel Economy, Durability, Resale Value

There are three operating-cost arguments that drive an Iranian household toward a Toyota or Hyundai/Kia and away from a locally-assembled Chinese crossover, and they are measurable.

First, fuel economy. The current consensus among Iranian taxi drivers and corporate fleet operators is that a compact Japanese sedan with a naturally-aspirated 1.5 to 1.8 litre engine returns five to six litres per 100 kilometres in Tehran traffic, while the typical Chinese-assembled small SUV with a 1.5 turbo returns eight to ten. The gap is thirty to fifty per cent, and at the new fuel pricing tiers inside Iran — where the government-supplied quota is still cheap but every litre above the quota is roughly sixteen times the quota price — the gap is paid out in cash every month. A taxi driver covering 1,000 km a month saves 30 to 50 litres of premium-priced fuel by running the smaller, lighter Japanese car. At Tehran street prices that is a meaningful share of a working-class monthly food budget.

Second, durability and repair simplicity. Iranian workshops are calibrated to Japanese cars from three decades of accumulated practice. A 2007 Toyota Corolla can be diagnosed, partly disassembled and reassembled on the side of the road with basic hand tools. The same is not true of a 2023 Chery Tiggo 7 assembled at the SAIPA plant, where body-panel gaps vary unit to unit, the wiring loom is locally sourced, and the diagnostic port speaks a protocol that most independent workshops do not have the tool for. Spare parts for a 2010 Corolla in Tehran's basements are still readily available. Spare parts for a 2023 Tiggo 7 CKD, in some configurations, are not.

Third, residual value. The Iranian second-hand market prices Japanese cars at a structural premium that the rial's decline has only widened. A 2014 Corolla bought new for 600 million rial in 2014 sells for 35 to 40 billion rial today, because that is what the market will pay for a vehicle that still has parts availability and a known reliability profile. A 2019 Chinese-assembled sedan of equivalent new price is not priced the same way. In an environment where the local currency is losing a meaningful share of its value every quarter, the choice of new car is in part a bet on which car will still be liquid in five years. Japanese is the safer bet.

4. The 2026 Supply Squeeze: Hormuz Disruptions and Toyota's Middle East Production Cuts

The wholesale lane to Iran is not a stable flow. It is a flow that depends on Toyota, Nissan and Hyundai's Middle East production remaining above a certain floor, and in 2026 that floor has been missed twice. The first cut came after shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz earlier in the year — Toyota announced a production adjustment for the Middle East market, with the cumulative scale running into the tens of thousands of units. The second cut was smaller but timed worse: it landed at the moment Iranian dealers were refilling inventory ahead of the late-2026 wedding season. Several Tehran distributors have reported waiting more than two months for replacement vehicles from the official Toyota channel. Some of them have rebooked into the Chinese-port wholesale lane, paying roughly the same landed cost as the official importer, and accepting a different documentary profile in exchange for delivery certainty.

The result is a market in which the official channels are running short and the wholesale channels are running hot. The market signal is no different from any other supply-constrained commodity: price-discovery happens where stock actually moves, and in 2026 that means the cross-border lane more than the official one.

5. What Iran's Import Lists Actually Show: Toyota and Nissan Reappearing in 2025-2026

It is a common misreading, in wholesale marketing, to assume that because Japan and Iran do not have a fully normalised trade relationship, no Japanese complete vehicles enter Iran. They do, and the official import lists published through 2025 and 2026 confirm it. The 2025 import list included Toyota and Nissan badged vehicles registered for sale inside Iran, and the July 2026 update added another round of Toyota and Nissan models. The volumes are small in absolute terms — Iran is not running a quota of 50,000 Japanese cars a year the way the Gulf states do — but the precedent is the relevant fact. The official import window is open, and the wholesale lane is the unofficial extension of that window for distributors who need more volume than the official channel can supply on a reliable schedule.

6. The Paradox of Official Channels vs Ground-Reality Demand

What an Iranian dealer on a Tehran sidewalk sees is not the same as what the Iranian customs data shows. The customs data shows a small stream of officially imported Japanese complete vehicles. The Tehran dealership reality is a continuous demand for Japanese badged stock at a price point the official channel cannot serve on a steady schedule, and a secondary market of high-mileage used Japanese cars imported through neighbouring jurisdictions and consolidated for sale inside Iran. The wholesale lane out of Chinese ports serves both flows: the official dealer who needs a 2026 model he cannot get from the official Toyota allocation, and the larger secondary-market consolidator who needs bulk supply. The pricing between the two flows has narrowed in 2026, which is itself a signal that the wholesale channel has become the effective marginal source.

7. Sourcing Japanese and Korean Badged Vehicles from China Ports: Models, Prices, Terms

For a wholesale distributor serving the Iranian market, the practical answer in 2026 is to source Japanese and Korean badged vehicles out of Chinese ports — Khorgos dry port on the Kazakhstan/China border for the overland route through Central Asia, and Nansha port in Guangzhou for the deep-water route via the Gulf. The documentary profile is the standard export commercial invoice, packing list, certificate of origin, and a buyer-nominated destination port — which the buyer is responsible for handling in line with their own jurisdiction's import and sanctions rules.

8. Hybrid as the Sweet Spot for Fuel-Scarce Markets

One of the most useful pieces of intelligence for any distributor weighing the Iranian route in 2026 is the technical fit of the hybrid powertrain. Iran's fuel problem is not theoretical. The country imports roughly fourteen to fifteen million litres of refined gasoline per day more than it can produce, and the public distribution network cannot make up the gap. Pure EVs are not a solution in the current infrastructure context: Iran's grid is ageing, residential supply is intermittent, and there is essentially no public charging network. The fit that the operating data points toward is the hybrid — both the conventional hybrid (HEV) such as the Toyota Hybrid System II fitted to the Corolla, Corolla Cross, Frontlander and the RAV4 2.0L Hybrid, and the dual-engine setup on the RAV4 2.5L AWD. HEV returns real-world economy in the five to six litres per 100 km range even under Tehran traffic, charges no external infrastructure, and the service network for the Toyota hybrid system in Iran is already established.

For a distributor pricing the Iran-bound container, the practical recommendation is a 60/40 mix of HEV trims to petrol-only trims, with the HEV carrying the higher FOB premium and the petrol-only trims carrying the higher unit volume. That mix tracks the underlying demand structure: a smaller but price-insensitive premium HEV segment that wants the fuel-economy story, and a larger price-sensitive base segment that wants the Toyota nameplate at the lowest entry price.

9. Compliance First: What Exporters and Buyers Must Verify

A wholesale guide for the Iranian market is not complete without an explicit statement on compliance. The export of passenger vehicles to Iran is governed by a layered set of rules that vary by jurisdiction of origin, jurisdiction of transhipment, and jurisdiction of the buyer. United States-origin components, software and finance channels may attract separate OFAC rules regardless of where the vehicle is finally delivered. European Union export controls apply separately. The buyer's own sanctions and import licensing rules in their jurisdiction are the buyer's responsibility to verify, not the seller's. A standard cross-border wholesale transaction between a Chinese port and an Iranian buyer will typically be documented under a third-country finance and insurance structure, and the legal characterisation of that transaction is not a matter a wholesale export desk should be giving legal advice on.

Globalucar's standing position is to deliver vehicles to the buyer-nominated destination port under the standard ICC Incoterms 2020 terms the buyer selects, against the buyer's letter of credit or an equivalent instrument, with the buyer responsible for import licensing, sanctions verification and customs clearance in the destination jurisdiction. Buyers and importers must independently verify applicable sanctions, export-control and import regulations for their destination market and consult qualified trade-compliance counsel before any booking. That is not boilerplate: in 2026 it is the most important sentence on this page.

10. Frequently Asked Questions

Why are Japanese cars back at the centre of the Iranian market in 2026?

Three operating pressures — a fourteen-to-fifteen-million-litre daily gasoline shortfall, a rial at 1,810,000 per dollar, and an aging fleet of pre-2015 Toyota and Hyundai/Kia nameplates — combined with two Toyota Middle East production cuts in 2026 to make Japanese badged vehicles the most resilient and most liquid hard asset in the Iranian passenger market. The Iranian vice president for energy optimisation, Esfahjani, summarised the household-level logic on national television on 16 August 2026: locally-assembled Chinese cars are "unreasonably priced, with poor quality stability and high running cost", whereas importing Japanese complete vehicles "would have given citizens a better driving experience and a lower total cost". The wholesale market is responding to that calculation regardless of the political framing.

How much Japanese badged stock is actually reaching Iran today?

Two streams run in parallel. The official import list published by the Iranian customs authority in 2025 and updated in July 2026 includes Toyota and Nissan badged vehicles, in limited but recurring volumes. The unofficial cross-border wholesale lane out of Chinese ports runs in addition to that, in larger volumes and on a different documentary profile. The two streams together now account for a small but growing share of the Iranian passenger market, while Chinese CKD-assembly brands such as Geely have exited the country in 2026 and Changan's joint project with SAIPA has been wound down.

Can a wholesale buyer in China actually source Toyota badged vehicles?

Yes. Toyota badged vehicles are produced for the global market, and the Chinese dealer network supplies wholesale quantities to certified export channels on a recurring basis. The constraint is not supply; the constraint is documentary. Each Toyota, Hyundai or Kia badged vehicle for export out of China carries the standard export commercial invoice, packing list, certificate of origin, and the manufacturer-issued export documentation that the buyer's destination jurisdiction may require. Pricing as of October 2026 ranges from USD 11,200 (Hyundai Elantra 2023 1.5L CVT GLX Elite FOB Khorgos) to USD 25,400 (Toyota RAV4 2026 2.0L Hybrid AWD) per unit, FOB or EXW depending on the port.

What is the right port to ship from for the Iranian market?

Two options. Nansha port in Guangzhou is the deep-water option for the Gulf route, with onward shipping to Bandar Abbas and the southern Iranian coast. Khorgos dry port on the Kazakhstan/China border is the overland option for cross-border consolidation through Central Asia. The Khorgos lane is typically used for higher-volume sedan runs where the per-unit inland cost is amortised across four to five vehicles per 40HQ. The Nansha lane is typically used for mixed sedan/SUV containers, premium trims, and buyers who need the original B/L straight from a deep-water port.

Why is hybrid the right answer for Iran in 2026?

Iran's fuel shortage is structural and will not be resolved by changes in the global oil price. The country imports roughly fourteen to fifteen million litres of refined gasoline per day more than it can produce, and the public distribution network is constrained. Pure EVs are not a solution because Iran's grid is ageing and there is essentially no public charging infrastructure. The hybrid — both the conventional HEV on the Toyota Hybrid System II and the dual-engine setup on the RAV4 2.5L AWD — returns five to six litres per 100 km in real-world Tehran traffic, charges no external infrastructure, and benefits from a Toyota hybrid service network in Iran that already exists.

What does a wholesale buyer need to verify before booking?

Three things, in this order. First, the buyer's own jurisdiction's import licensing and sanctions rules — including any U.S. OFAC reach, any EU export-control rules, and any destination-country registration requirements. Second, the documentary profile of the transaction — Incoterms 2020 terms, letter of credit or equivalent instrument, third-country finance and insurance if applicable. Third, the technical fit of the vehicle to the destination market's operating environment — fuel availability, parts pipeline, local workshop compatibility, residual value. Globalucar will support the documentary and technical side of the booking; the legal characterisation of the transaction is a matter for the buyer's own trade-compliance counsel.

Brake parts filled more floor space at Phase 1 of the 140th Canton Fair than any vehicle category except the complete-vehicle assembly booths — and the fair's own numbers explain why: the organizer reported 189,000 overseas buyers from 214 countries and regions by the close on 19 October, up 13.3 percent on the previous session. If you source brake pads, rotors or calipers for Toyota, Hyundai or Kia applications, this is the one window each year where the supply chain stands in five halls along the Pearl River. This guide walks the brake aisle the way a working buyer should — from the halls to OE numbers, friction mixes, markings, FOB bands and MOQs.

Why Brake Parts Own the Phase 1 Floor

Phase 1, themed Advanced Manufacturing, covered 520,000 square meters with more than 25,000 booths and over 12,000 participating enterprises across 19 exhibition areas — and the vehicles-and-auto-parts sections sit inside that block. For a brake buyer the density matters more than the headline area: within one aisle you can compare a pad factory, a friction-mix blender, a rotor casting plant and a caliper machining shop.

The audience is there for the same reason. A record 189,000 overseas buyers attended Phase 1 in person, and the biggest contingencies came from the markets where brake parts move fastest: the Middle East, Africa, Southeast Asia and South America, where the vehicle parc is dominated by Corolla, Camry, Hilux, Elantra, Accent, Sportage and Cerato platforms running for a decade or more. Old fleets consume friction — that is the trade in one sentence.

One scheduling note that catches buyers each session: auto parts appear only in Phase 1. Phase 2 (23–27 October) shifts to consumer goods and building materials, and Phase 3 (31 October–4 November) covers textiles, toys and food. During the 20–22 October changeover break the halls are dark, but the suppliers are not, and the online platform stays open year-round. Our guide to the auto parts halls at Pazhou maps the brake sections for next session.

What the Brake Aisle Actually Carries

Walk the vehicle-parts sections and the brake offering sorts into four families, each rewarding a different inspection routine. A pad maker with its own friction formulation is not the same animal as a rotor machining house buying castings from a foundry — and the booth tells you which one you are facing.

Product familyBooth displayWhat to inspect by handTypical MOQ

Brake rotors and drumsPainted, coated and bare discs; vented and solid; drum stacksSurface finish, balance drill marks, coating coverage, runout tolerance on the drawing100–300 pcs per part number
Calipers and loaded calipersRemanufactured and new units; pistons, seals and brackets separatePiston bore finish, bleeder thread condition, bracket casting integrity50–200 pcs per part number
Hardware and sensorsShim kits, guide pins, wear sensors in poly bagsClip spring tension, sensor connector type for your market500–1,000 sets

Notice what the MOQ column implies. A buyer building a mixed container across twenty applications hits factory minimums easily; one who wants six rotors for a niche Corolla variant cannot, not at factory pricing. This is why consolidation — mixing applications inside one supplier's range, or suppliers inside one container — is the real negotiation, long before anyone argues over unit price.

Friction Materials: Matching the Mix to Your Market

The first question a pad booth will ask is which friction material you want — a shrug costs you later in warranty claims. The three mainstream families trade noise, dust, fade resistance and cost against each other.

Friction mix baseSteel wool and metal fibers, 30–65% metal contentCeramic fibers, filler and bonding resins, little exposed metalOrganic mix with 10–30% metal additions

Two market notes suppliers will confirm if pressed. In Gulf and Sahel markets, semi-metallic holds the volume because fleets replace pads on interval and dust is tolerated; ceramic sells at the retail counter where the end customer pays. Southeast Asian urban fleets are drifting toward ceramic for ride comfort. Run both mixes on your top three applications with a local installer before you commit a container.

Walk In With OE Numbers, Not Part Descriptions

Every booth keeps a catalogue indexed by OE reference number, not by the phrase "pads for a 2016 Corolla." A buyer who opens with OE numbers gets a different conversation: the salesperson checks stock, confirms the tooling, quotes a concrete price, and says within minutes whether the part ships from warehouse or needs a production run. A buyer who opens with a description gets a "please send the application list" and a three-day wait for an email that may never arrive.

The filter runs deeper than speed. A factory with real coverage on Toyota, Hyundai and Kia brake applications answers OE-number questions instantly, because those numbers are already in its mould list. A trading company reselling catalogues asks you to wait while it checks with "the engineer." That hesitation sorts the floor faster than any certificate on the wall. Our OE parts library carries reference numbers across Toyota, Hyundai and Kia brake applications, and our guide on verifying suppliers with certificates, OE numbers and factory audits shows how to turn a booth conversation into a documented answer.

Reading a Brake Quotation: FOB, MOQ and the Fine Print

The quotations that follow the fair are where value is won or lost, and brake quotations have their own hiding places.
