content:
A valve cover gasket is a rubber ring that costs less than a tank of fuel, and a failed one can still take a coil pack, a catalytic converter and a weekend with it. The part is simple; the diagnosis is not. Oil that appears at the top of an engine can come from the cover gasket, the spark plug tube seals, a cracked plastic cover, a clogged PCV system or a head gasket that is about to cost ten times more to fix. This guide separates those cases, gives the torque numbers that actually prevent repeat failures, and lists the OE references we hold for BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Toyota and Lexus applications.

What the Valve Cover Gasket Actually Seals

The valve cover sits on top of the cylinder head and closes the chamber where the camshafts, valves, springs and lifters live. The gasket between cover and head keeps splash-fed oil inside that chamber and keeps dust out. That is the whole job — and the limits of the job explain most of the confusion around it.

It does not seal combustion pressure. It does not separate coolant from oil. It is not exposed to the several hundred degrees and dozens of bar that a head gasket survives every cycle. A valve cover gasket works at low pressure and moderate temperature, which is why the material is usually rubber — EPDM, HNBR or silicone — rather than the multi-layer steel used lower down the engine. On older engines the gasket is a flat cork or rubber sheet; on anything built in the last twenty years it is a moulded rubber profile that clips into a groove around the cover, often with separate tube seals pressed into the cover for each spark plug well.

That design detail matters commercially. The gasket is a consumable that gets replaced whenever the top end is opened — during a timing chain job, a camshaft sensor replacement, a valve clearance service or a spark plug change on an engine with oil in the wells. Shops that keep a small range on the shelf sell them steadily; importers who stock only complete gasket sets miss the single-line demand from workshops that already have the rest of the kit.

Seven Symptoms, Ranked by What They Actually Mean

Owners describe the same failure in different words, and the words point at different stages of it. The table below sorts the common reports by what each one tells a technician.

What the driver reportsWhat you find on inspectionWhat it usually meansHow urgent
"There is oil on the engine"Wet sheen or dark crust along the cover-to-head seam, heaviest at the rear or near the cam sensorEarly external leak; gasket hardening, cover still flatPlan within weeks
"It smells like burning oil after I park"Oil dripped onto the exhaust manifold or downpipe; light smoke from the engine bayLeak has reached a hot surface — the smell is the leak rate talkingPlan within days
"It misfires when cold"Oil pooled in one or more spark plug wells; coil boot swollen and softTube seals have failed, not just the perimeter gasketRepair now
Check engine light with P0300–P0304Oil-fouled plug, tracking marks on the boot, misfire counter climbing on one bankOil is shorting the ignition circuit; the gasket is the root causeRepair now, before the converter suffers
"It uses oil but never drips"No puddle, but consumption above roughly one quart per 1,000 miles and a wet rear seamLeak is burning off on the manifold instead of reaching the groundDiagnose within a week
"The belt squeals"Oil mist on the accessory belt, tensioner or alternatorLong-running leak contaminating rubber and electricsRepair now; belt may need replacing too
"It smells hot and there is smoke"Heavy baked-on oil, sometimes smoke from the turbo or manifold area after shutdownAdvanced leak close to an exhaust componentStop driving; assess fire risk

Two of these symptoms are routinely misread. A misfire on a car with a known oil leak is usually blamed on the coil, and the coil does get replaced — then fails again, because the oil in the well was never addressed. And low oil consumption with no puddle gets filed under "old engine" when the leak is simply landing somewhere hot. Both misreads cost more than the gasket.

Valve Cover Gasket or Head Gasket? The Test That Settles It

This is the question that decides whether a customer faces a two-hour job or a cylinder-head removal, and the two failures share almost no symptoms once you look at the fluids rather than the oil.

SignalValve cover gasketHead gasket
Where the leak startsTop of the engine, at the cover-to-head seamLower down, at the block-to-head joint; often invisible from above
Fluid involvedEngine oil onlyCoolant, oil, or combustion gas — rarely just one
Coolant levelUnchangedDrops without an external leak; bubbles in the expansion tank
ExhaustNormal, or light blue smoke from the engine bayPersistent white, sweet-smelling steam from the tailpipe
Oil conditionClean or normally dirtyMilky, coffee-coloured emulsion on the dipstick or filler cap
TemperatureNormalOverheats, or the heater runs cold then hot
Typical repairGasket kit and 1.5–6 hours of labourCylinder head removal, surfacing, new bolts — days in the shop

If coolant is disappearing, the oil looks like milkshake, or the temperature gauge climbs, stop diagnosing the cover gasket and pressure-test the cooling system. If none of those three is present and the oil is at the top of the engine, the cover gasket is the right suspect. A combustion-gas test on the coolant bottle takes ten minutes and settles the question before anyone orders parts.

Why They Fail: Heat, Pressure and the Wrong Wrench

Four causes account for most failures we see in warranty returns, and only one of them is the gasket's own fault.

Heat cycling. Rubber that is squeezed between an aluminium head and a hot cover takes a permanent set over thousands of cycles. It hardens, loses elasticity, and stops following the small movements of a cover that expands at a different rate from the head. This is normal ageing, and it is why the part fails on time rather than on mileage.

Crankcase pressure. A blocked PCV valve, a collapsed breather hose or a turbo engine with worn rings pushes pressure into the cover. The gasket is not designed to hold positive pressure, so it lifts at the weakest point — usually the rear of the cover, where nobody looks. Replacing the gasket without checking the PCV system is the most common cause of a leak that returns within a month.

Over-torque. Valve cover bolts are small, usually M6, and the specification is 8–12 Nm on most engines — about the force of a firm wrist, not a ratchet handle. Tightening beyond that crushes the gasket profile and distorts a plastic cover. The leak that appears three months after a "quick" gasket job is almost always an over-torqued one.

Warped or cracked covers. Plastic covers on modern turbo engines move and crack with age; aluminium covers warp if they have been overheated. A straightedge and feeler gauge across the sealing face takes a minute and prevents a repeat repair. If the cover is out of flat, no gasket will seal it, and the correct part to sell is the complete cover with gasket fitted.

How Long Should One Last?

Published service life clusters between 60,000 and 120,000 miles, with most workshops quoting 60,000 to 100,000 miles as the realistic window. Treat those figures as a planning horizon, not a service interval — no manufacturer schedules valve cover gasket replacement, because the part is replaced when it leaks, and the spread between a 60,000-mile failure and a 150,000-mile one is driven by conditions rather than design.

Three conditions shorten the window predictably. Sustained high ambient temperature hardens rubber faster, so fleets in the Gulf, North Africa and South Asia see earlier failures than the same engine in a temperate market. Engines that already burn oil coat the gasket in hot vapour and degrade it from both sides. And any engine with a marginal PCV system pressurises the cover continuously. In those three cases, inspection at every oil change is worth more than any mileage rule.

For a workshop, the practical instruction to give a customer is simple: check the seam and the plug wells at every service, and replace when you find fresh oil — not when a number on a chart says so.

The Tube Seals Nobody Quotes

Most modern covers carry four separate tube seals — one per spark plug well — pressed into the cover, and they fail at roughly the same age as the perimeter gasket. When they do, oil fills the well from below, the coil boot sits in it, and the spark shorts down the insulator instead of jumping the gap.

The commercial consequence is a second repair. A shop that orders only the perimeter gasket discovers the wells are full during reassembly, and either reuses the old seals or pulls the cover again a month later. Complete kits include the tube seals and the cover grommets for the bolt holes, and they cost a few dollars more. Any engine with oil in the wells should also have the affected coil boots inspected; a swollen, soft boot will keep misfiring even with a dry well.

Torque, Sequence and Sealant: The Install Rules That Matter

Installation errors cause more comebacks than material defects. The procedure below is the one that holds across BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Toyota and Lexus four-cylinder and six-cylinder engines; confirm the exact figure in the workshop manual for the engine in front of you, because the pattern and the spec do vary.

1. Clean the mating surfaces completely. Old gasket residue, cured sealant and oil film all prevent the new profile from seating. Solvent and a plastic scraper, then a lint-free cloth — no abrasive disc on an aluminium head.

2. Check the cover for flatness. Straightedge and feeler gauge across the sealing face; a plastic cover that rocks or shows a gap needs replacing, not resealing.

3. Fit the gasket dry. Modern moulded gaskets seat in the cover groove without sealant. The only exception is a small dab of RTV at the corners where the cover meets a separate cam cap or timing cover, where the manual calls for it. Sealant anywhere else, especially in an oil drain-back passage, can block an oil feed.

4. Hand-thread every bolt first. Threading by hand prevents cross-threading and stops the cover being pulled off-centre as the first bolt tightens.

5. Torque in three passes, centre outward, in a cross pattern. Roughly 30 percent, 70 percent, then full value — typically 8–12 Nm for M6 bolts, with some engines specifying 7–10 Nm. A torque wrench is not optional here; the difference between sealed and crushed is a few newton-metres.

6. Reassemble and verify. Refit coils to their original wells, reconnect the PCV and breather hoses, run the engine for five minutes, then inspect the seam with a torch. Recheck after 50 miles, when the gasket has taken its first heat cycle.

Two things not to do: never reuse a gasket that has been compressed, and never pour in a stop-leak product to buy time. Stop-leak swells rubber briefly and then deposits in oil passages and the heater matrix, which turns a cheap repair into an expensive one.

Cost is driven almost entirely by how much has to come off to reach the cover. The ranges below reflect parts plus labour in a typical independent workshop; dealer pricing runs higher, and markets with expensive labour skew toward the top of each band.

Buying Valve Cover Gaskets Wholesale from Guangzhou

Three decisions shape the order, and each one has a failure mode worth knowing before the container is booked.

Gasket only, or complete kit. The kit — perimeter gasket, tube seals, bolt grommets — is the version that sells to workshops, because it matches the labour already being charged. Single gaskets sell to price-driven retail and to shops that already hold seals. Stock roughly 70 percent kits and 30 percent single gaskets unless your customers tell you otherwise.

Material and hardness. HNBR and silicone handle heat better than basic EPDM, and the price difference is cents per piece, not dollars. Ask for the compound and the hardness on the datasheet; a supplier who cannot name the compound is buying on price from someone else. For Gulf and African markets, specify the higher-temperature compound and say so on the label.

Packing and mixed loads. Gaskets are light and bulky, so they combine well with heavier parts in a mixed container — a natural fit for a buyer already shipping brake or suspension lines. Flat-packing in labelled poly bags with the OE number printed on each bag saves hours at the receiving end, and it is the kind of detail that separates a warehouse-ready supplier from one that ships loose pieces.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I drive with a leaking valve cover gasket?
Short term, yes — but the clock is not free. Oil dripping onto the exhaust manifold burns and smokes, oil in the spark plug wells causes misfires that can destroy a catalytic converter, and a leak near the turbo or manifold carries a fire risk. Treat a slow external seep as a repair to schedule within weeks, and a leak that has reached a hot surface or the plug wells as a repair to do now.

How do I know it is the cover gasket and not the head gasket?
Check three things: coolant level, oil colour and exhaust. A valve cover gasket leaks oil only, leaves the coolant level alone and does not overheat the engine. A head gasket typically loses coolant with no visible drip, turns the oil milky, sends white sweet smoke out of the tailpipe and pushes the temperature gauge up. A combustion-gas test on the coolant settles it in ten minutes.

Do I need to replace the whole valve cover?
Only if the cover is warped, cracked or its sealing face is out of flat — common on plastic covers fitted to modern turbo engines. On an aluminium cover that passes a straightedge check, the gasket and tube seals are enough. Replacing a gasket on a warped cover guarantees a repeat leak.

How long does the job take?
An inline four with the cover accessible runs 1.5–2 hours. A V6 where the intake has to come off runs 4–6 hours. Add time for cleaning, and add the cost of a new cover if flatness fails.

Can I reuse the old gasket or seal it with RTV?
No on both counts. A compressed gasket has taken a permanent set and will not seal again, and sealant on a moulded rubber profile prevents it seating in its groove. RTV belongs only at the corners where the manual specifies it. Stop-leak additives are worse — they swell the rubber briefly, then clog oil passages.

What is the minimum order for wholesale supply?
Fifty pieces per reference. Kits and single gaskets can be mixed within one order, and gaskets combine well with brake, cooling or suspension parts in a mixed container. Quotations are issued FOB Guangzhou, usually within 48 hours of receiving the OE list.

content:
A booth, a business card and a glossy catalogue do not make a supplier. When you source auto parts at the Canton Fair, the real work is verifying that the company in front of you actually makes the part, holds the certifications it claims, and cross-references OE numbers accurately enough that the shipment fits the vehicles your customers drive. With the 140th session’s auto-parts-relevant Phase 1 running 15–19 October 2026 at the Pazhou complex in Guangzhou, this guide gives you a repeatable workflow — the license check, the certification check, the OE number check, the on-booth sample review and the factory audit — that separates real manufacturers from well-dressed intermediaries. Run it before you wire a deposit, and a five-day fair becomes a five-day confirmation exercise instead of a five-day guessing game.

How to Verify an Auto Parts Supplier at Canton Fair: The Big Picture

Verifying a supplier is not one question but five, and each one answers a different risk. The license check confirms the company exists and is legally allowed to manufacture. The certification check confirms its quality system and product performance meet automotive standards. The OE number check confirms the part will fit the vehicle it claims to replace. The sample and test-report review confirms the goods match the paperwork. The factory audit confirms the operation behind the booth is real and repeatable.

Buyers who skip this work at the fair usually do it later, at a much higher price. A wrong cross-reference does not fail on the test bench; it fails at the customer’s workshop, generating returns, claims and lost accounts. A trading company posing as a factory adds a margin layer without adding capability. A missing or expired certificate becomes your compliance problem the moment the container clears customs. Roughly speaking, a first container order that goes wrong can cost more than ten proper audits — which is exactly why the verification workflow belongs at the booth, before any deposit leaves your account.

The good news is that most of this takes minutes per supplier, not days. The sections below are ordered the way an experienced buyer actually works a hall.

Start With the License: Factory or Trading Company?

Ask for the business license first, and photograph it. On a Chinese license the unified social credit code is an 18-character code that can be checked against the national enterprise credit system, and the business scope will state whether the company is licensed for production (生产) or only for trading. A genuine factory shows a scope that includes manufacturing; a trading company typically shows distribution or import/export. That single field settles the most common source of confusion at any trade show.

Do not stop at the paper. Cross-check the registered address against satellite imagery: a factory footprint with truck docks and rooftops looks nothing like an office tower. If the address on the license does not match the address on the business card, ask why. Legitimate multi-site manufacturers exist, but the answer should be specific and verifiable, not vague.

SignalLooks like a factoryLooks like a trading company
Business scopeLists production / manufacturingLists trading, distribution, import-export
Process ownershipNames the machines and processes it runs (forging, CNC, heat treatment)Cannot name a process it owns
Sample originOffers a unit pulled from the production lineSample arrives from “a partner factory”
Address checkSatellite shows a plant and loading docksSatellite shows an office or virtual address
Capacity mathHeadcount, lines and monthly output add upLarge “capacity” with no verifiable equipment

Trading companies are not automatically a problem. Some curate excellent factories and add real value on consolidation and logistics. The problem is misrepresentation: paying factory pricing for trader service, or discovering months later that your “manufacturer” never controlled quality at all. Knowing which one you are dealing with lets you price and protect the order correctly.

Certifications That Matter: IATF 16949, ECE R90 and What to Verify

Certificates are where buyers are most often fooled, because a logo is easy to print and a system is hard to run. Ask for the certificate number, the scope, the issuing body and the expiry date — not an image of a badge. IATF 16949, the automotive industry’s core quality management standard, can be checked on the IATF’s public certification database, and certificates are re-audited on a three-year cycle. An expired certificate is meaningless. A supplier who answers a request for IATF 16949 with a generic ISO 9001 certificate is telling you something: ISO 9001 is a general quality standard with far lighter requirements for automotive production and is not a substitute for safety-critical parts.

CertificateWhat it coversHow to verify
IATF 16949Automotive quality management system; process control, traceability, internal auditsAsk for cert number, scope, expiry and issuing body; check the IATF public database
ISO 9001Generic quality management; not automotive-specificAcceptable only as a supplement, never a substitute for IATF 16949 on safety parts
ECE R90Brake pad performance for the aftermarket; replacement must sit within a defined tolerance band of the OE partAsk which dynamometer and test house ran it; in-house capability signals stronger control
ECE R13 / R10 / R118Braking systems (R13), electromagnetic compatibility (R10), interior material flammability (R118)Match the regulation to the part category; request the test report, not the claim

Note a live change in the rules: the IATF’s updated certification rules took effect on 1 January 2025 and extend IATF 16949 scope toward aftermarket replacement parts by 2028. In practice this means the line between “OEM” and “aftermarket” certifications is narrowing, and buyers who verify certifications today are building a checklist that stays relevant for years. For brake pads specifically, ECE R90 approval means the part was tested on an approved dynamometer and must not deviate beyond a fixed percentage from the OE pad’s performance curve — a supplier that outsources this testing has slower validation and less control than one that runs it in-house.

OE Numbers: The Buyer's Secret Weapon for Fitment Verification

The single most useful thing you can carry into a hall is a clean OE number list. OE numbers are the shared language between your vehicle data and the factory’s cross-reference file, and they are the fastest way to test whether a supplier actually knows fitment or is guessing from photos. Provide the OE numbers for the vehicles you service — for example a Toyota brake pad reference such as 04465-35030, a Hyundai/Kia number in the 58101-xxxxx family for front pads, or a Denso and Bosch reference on an electrical part — and ask the supplier to confirm fitment with documented evidence.

A reliable supplier maintains a cross-reference database that maps its own SKU to OE references from vehicle makers and from tier-one brands, and can produce a specification sheet confirming dimensional and performance data for each reference. Treat every OE cross-reference as indicative until verified against the vehicle’s VIN or your own fitment catalogue. Two distinctions matter: a single aftermarket part number often replaces several OE numbers that share one core specification, which is a real inventory advantage for distributors — but the consolidation must be technically valid, not merely convenient. And “OE replacement” (a direct physical and functional substitute) is a stronger claim than “OE equivalent,” which can hide a different friction material or specification. Always confirm the material and specification match in writing.

Cross-reference accuracy has a maintenance cost. New models and mid-cycle updates arrive every year, so a serious supplier updates its fitment data on a rolling basis, often quarterly. Ask when their database was last refreshed. A supplier still quoting a 2019 cross-reference file is a supplier whose errors will land on your returns desk.

What to Check on the Booth Floor: Samples, Tolerances and Test Reports

At the booth, work through the physical evidence in a fixed order so nothing is skipped when the hall gets busy:

  1. Pull a production sample, not a display sample. Ask for a unit from the current production run and check the part number stamped on the product itself, not just the catalogue page. Confirm the stamped number matches the quoted OE reference.
  2. Measure what matters. Carry a caliper. On a brake pad, check backing plate thickness and the friction material edge; on a suspension arm, confirm critical dimensions against your drawing. A part that is dimensionally off by a fraction will pass a visual check and fail on the vehicle.
  3. Ask for the test report, not the test claim. A dated report naming the test method and the lab beats any verbal assurance. For chassis and brake parts, request material test reports matched to the production lot so a future complaint can be traced back to a specific batch.
  4. Review packaging and marking. Correct part numbers, bilingual labelling where your market requires it, and lot or date codes are signs of a controlled process. Mismatched numbers between listing and product are a classic warning sign.

Record a short voice memo at every booth before you move on: company name, hall and booth number, what you saw, what they promised. By day three the halls blur together, and that memo chain becomes your follow-up database when you sit down to rank suppliers.

Factory Audits: Announced, Unannounced and Third-Party Options

A booth conversation verifies intent; an audit verifies reality. There are three practical ways to run one, and the strongest programs use a mix.

  • Announced audit. The supplier knows you are coming and prepares documents, payroll records and certificates. This is necessary for document-heavy checks and gives you a structured, comparable report — but a prepared factory can also stage its floor.
  • Unannounced spot check. Book a flight and do not notify the factory. Arrive at the gate, present your card and ask for the plant manager. Worker count, running lines and shift activity tell you the truth that a scheduled visit cannot. If the factory initially refuses entry, record that refusal as a finding.
  • Third-party audit. Independent firms such as SGS, Bureau Veritas, Intertek and QIMA run capability, compliance and quality-system audits and report directly to you with photos. A basic verification audit commonly runs around USD 200–500, a fuller technical quality audit higher, with the largest international firms at the top of the range. Guangdong is one of the more expensive regions, but it is also where a large share of auto parts capacity sits.

Watch the cost benchmark as a share of your spend. For most importers, a sensible audit budget is a small fraction of what they spend with a given supplier each year — cheap insurance against a single failed container. And remember that an audit is a snapshot: even a factory that passes every step can slip when raw material prices move or a key operator leaves. Treat verification as the beginning of monitoring, not a one-time pass.

Pre-Shipment Inspection vs Factory Audit: What Each One Catches

Buyers often use these two terms interchangeably, but they answer different questions and catch different failures.

DimensionFactory auditPre-shipment inspection (PSI)
Question answeredCan this factory make my parts well and honestly, over the long term?Is this specific batch ready to ship?
What it reviewsEquipment, process control, QC systems, traceability, complianceThe goods against the purchase order, at 80–100% production complete
MethodOn-site walkthrough, records, worker interviewsAQL sampling of the produced batch, dimensional and functional checks
TimingBefore you commit; typically one day on siteBefore container loading, every first order and every risky order
Typical costBroadly USD 200–500 basic, higher for full technical auditsOften a few hundred USD per inspection

The practical rule: audit the factory once, inspect the goods every time. An audit without ongoing inspection still lets a bad batch through, and inspection without an audit still lets you buy from a trader with no production control. Together they cover the whole chain.

Red Flags: Ten Answers That Mean Walk Away

Verification is often about listening. The table below pairs the question with the answer a serious factory gives and the answer that should end the conversation.

QuestionGreen flagRed flag
“Send your certificate.”Cert number, scope, expiry, issuing bodyA logo image, or “we are certified”
“Do you make it or resell it?”Names the processes and machines it ownsVague, or “we have a partner factory”
“Show the test report.”Dated report, named lab, stated method“It always passes”
“What if a batch is out of spec?”Written RMA process and defect termsAssurances given only verbally
“Lead time at double volume?”Real lead time, name the bottleneck“Seven days, always”
“Can I see the line today?”Sends real-time footage or invites youExcuses, delays, stock photos
“Confirm this OE number.”Checks a database and sends the spec sheetConfirms from a photo alone
“Who pays for returns?”A clear warranty and defect-rate termThe topic changes
“What is the sample fee?”A paid sample and a small trial batchPressure to skip straight to the big order
“Can a third party inspect?”Yes, with full accessRefusal of third-party QC access

None of these answers is fatal on its own; a pattern of them is. A single fail on the license, certificate or reference check is reason to pause the order until it is resolved in writing.

A 5-Minute Verification Workflow You Can Run At the Fair

In a busy hall you will not have an hour per booth. Compress the workflow into five minutes and save the deep checks for your shortlist:

  1. Minute 1 — identity. Photograph the business license and card; note the credit code and the business scope.
  2. Minute 2 — certification. Request IATF 16949 with number, scope and expiry; note the issuing body for later verification.
  3. Minute 3 — fitment. Hand over three OE numbers from your list and ask for written confirmation with a spec sheet.
  4. Minute 4 — sample. Pull a production unit, photograph the stamped part number, and note one dimensional check you ran.
  5. Minute 5 — record. Voice-memo the booth, the promises and the next step. Mark the supplier shortlist, watch-list or drop.

Suppliers that clear all five minutes move to your audit list. Suppliers that stumble on any single minute move to the watch-list, where a written follow-up either resolves the gap or confirms the concern. This is the same discipline that makes hybrid sourcing between fairs work once you are back home.

After the Fair: Turning Verification into a Repeatable System

The fair is where verification starts, not where it ends. Within 48 hours of each hall day, convert every promising contact into a written record: restate the part numbers, quantities, FOB prices and agreed terms, and ask the supplier to confirm in writing. A supplier’s written confirmation is itself a quality filter — what they will not put in writing, they will not stand behind.

Then run sample validation against your golden sample, place a structured trial order small enough to limit risk but large enough to be taken seriously, and inspect it before it ships. If the supplier is in Guangdong, book a factory visit during the changeover break. Once an SKU is validated, move reorders to your fastest online channel and keep a cross-reference check in the loop, so fitment accuracy stays current as new model years arrive. Our OE parts library is a starting point for checking references, and a local partner can keep the verification rhythm going while you are 9,000 kilometres away.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I verify a Chinese auto parts supplier's IATF 16949 certificate?

Ask for the certificate number, the scope, the issuing certification body and the expiry date — not a badge image. Then check the number on the IATF’s public certification database. IATF 16949 certificates are re-audited on a three-year cycle, so an expired certificate is meaningless. If a supplier answers an IATF request with an ISO 9001 certificate, treat it as a warning sign: ISO 9001 is a general standard and is not a substitute for automotive production on safety-critical parts.

What is the fastest way to check if an auto part will fit my vehicle?

Use OE numbers. Send the supplier your OE references for the target vehicles and ask them to confirm fitment with documented evidence and a specification sheet. A reliable supplier maps its own SKU to OE references from vehicle makers and tier-one brands. Treat every cross-reference as indicative until it is verified against the vehicle’s VIN or your own fitment catalogue, and confirm whether the part is an “OE replacement” or merely “OE equivalent.”

Should I order a factory audit or a pre-shipment inspection?

Both, for different reasons. A factory audit checks whether the supplier can make your parts well and honestly over the long term — equipment, process control, QC systems and compliance. A pre-shipment inspection checks whether a specific batch is ready to ship, using AQL sampling at 80–100% production complete. Auditing the factory once and inspecting the goods every time covers both ends of the chain.

How much does a factory audit in China cost in 2026?

A basic verification audit commonly runs around USD 200–500, with fuller technical quality audits higher; the largest international firms such as SGS and Bureau Veritas price at the top of the range, and Guangdong sits among the more expensive regions. The right benchmark is not the absolute fee but the fee as a fraction of your annual spend with that supplier — a small slice is cheap insurance against one failed container.

How can I tell a factory from a trading company at the Canton Fair?

Three checks. First, the business license: the scope should include production, not only trading. Second, process ownership: a real factory can name the machines and processes it runs, such as forging, CNC machining, heat treatment and testing. Third, the sample: ask for a unit pulled from the current production line rather than a display piece, and confirm the part number stamped on the product matches the quoted reference.

What should I do in the first 48 hours after meeting a supplier at the fair?

Put everything in writing. Restate part numbers, quantities, FOB prices and agreed terms, and ask the supplier to confirm in writing — what they will not confirm in writing, they will not stand behind. Then run sample validation against your golden sample and place a structured trial order before committing to a full container. If the supplier is in Guangdong, book a factory visit during the changeover break while you are still in the region.

title: Water Pump vs Thermostat: Which One Is Overheating Your Engine?
description: Water pump or thermostat? Three checks that separate them, P0128 explained, replace-both rules, and 30 OE references for BMW, Mercedes-Benz and VW.

Why the Symptoms Overlap So Badly

Three Checks That Separate Them

Still Overheating After the Thermostat Was Changed

content:
A thermostat costs less than a brake pad and a water pump costs less than a headlight, yet between them they account for most of the overheating jobs that reach a workshop. Both fail in ways that look identical from the driver's seat, and the usual shortcut — replace both and hope — hides a third possibility that is far more expensive. This guide separates the two failures by what each part actually does, gives the three checks that settle the question without dismantling anything, and lists thirty OE references we hold for BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Volkswagen, Audi and Toyota applications.

Two Parts, Two Different Jobs

The cooling system is a loop, and the two components sit at opposite ends of it. The thermostat is a valve. It decides where coolant goes: through the engine only while the engine is cold, through the radiator once the coolant reaches its rated opening temperature. The water pump is the mover. It has no opinion about temperature; it simply pushes volume, and its output rises and falls with engine speed on a belt-driven design.

That split explains almost every diagnostic difference in this article. A thermostat failure changes when the engine reaches temperature. A pump failure changes whether heat leaves the engine at all.

The temperature at which the valve opens is stamped on the part, and it matters commercially. European petrol engines commonly run thermostats rated around 88–90 °C, with the whole range across passenger cars sitting roughly between 82 °C and 93 °C — about 180–200 °F. Normal operating temperature once warm sits higher, generally 90–105 °C. Fit a thermostat rated ten degrees low and the engine will run cold enough to set a fault code and raise fuel consumption, which is why a cheap substitution is never actually cheap.

Design has also moved. On older engines both parts are mechanical and belt-driven. On BMW’s N52, N54 and N55 six-cylinders the pump is electrically driven and controlled by the engine management, so there is no belt to watch and no pulley to wobble — the failure shows up as a stored fault code and a command test that produces no flow. Any diagnostic routine written before about 2005 will mislead a technician working on those engines.

Why the Symptoms Overlap So Badly

Three mechanisms blur the picture, and each one has fooled someone into replacing the wrong part.

No flow looks like no radiator. If the pump is not circulating, the radiator stays cool too — so a cold lower hose, the classic “thermostat is stuck shut” clue, can also mean a dead pump. The hose test is supporting evidence, not proof.

Air behaves like a broken component. A low coolant level or an incomplete bleed leaves a pocket at the temperature sensor or in the heater circuit. The gauge swings, the heater goes hot and cold, and the engine overheats under load — the same signature as a failing pump. Air is far more common than a failed pump on a car that has just had cooling work done.

The engine has more than two parts. A restricted radiator, a collapsed hose, a fan that never runs, a pressure cap that will not hold, or combustion gas entering the coolant will all produce overheating that no amount of pump and thermostat replacement will fix. Those are the cases that end up as a comeback, and they are the reason a pressure test belongs in the first ten minutes rather than the last.

The Symptom Matrix

Sorted by what the driver reports, with the component each pattern favours. Read the “more likely” column as a starting hypothesis, not a verdict.

Reported symptomMore likely partWhyConfirmation test
Warms up very slowly; gauge never reaches the middleThermostat stuck openCoolant circulates through the radiator from cold, so the engine never reaches ratingScan-tool warm-up curve plateaus below rating; upper hose warms early
Heats normally, then spikes several minutes after startThermostat stuck closedFlow to the radiator never opens; the bypass circuit keeps the heater working, which is why heat still feels fineUpper hose stays cold while the gauge climbs
Fine around town, overheats on the highway or under loadWater pump (impeller or flow)Heat rejection demand rises with load; a weak impeller cannot keep upTemperature rises with engine speed; heater output drops as revs rise
Overheats at idle, cools once movingNeither — usually fan or airflowRoad speed substitutes for the fan; the loop itself is soundCommand the fan on with a scan tool and watch the temperature fall
Coolant level drops, no puddle on the groundWater pump seal or weep holeSmall loss evaporates on a hot engine; dried residue rather than a poolCold pressure test; inspect the weep hole and the pump-to-block seam
Grinding or whining from the front of the engineWater pump bearingBearing wear is audible before it becomes a leak; pulley play followsIsolate the noise with the belt off; check for shaft play
Heater weak at idle, stronger with revsWater pump (low-speed flow)Heater core is the highest point in the loop and the first to notice reduced flowCompare heater outlet temperature at idle and at 2,000 rpm
Gauge swings repeatedly on one driveThermostat sticking intermittentlyA valve that hangs part-open produces temperature cycling rather than a single failureLog coolant temperature over a full drive; look for repeated sawtooth

The first two rows are the ones that get confused most often, and the confusion is expensive in the wrong direction: a stuck-closed thermostat still delivers cabin heat, so owners conclude the cooling system is working. By the time the gauge reaches the red, the head has already been heat-soaked.

Three Checks That Separate Them

None of these requires draining the system, and together they resolve most cases. Do all of them with the engine completely cold to start, and never open a pressurised cap.

One: watch the warm-up curve, not the dash gauge. Connect a scan tool and log engine coolant temperature from a cold start through fifteen minutes of driving. A healthy engine climbs steadily and levels off near the thermostat rating, then stabilises a little above it. A curve that plateaus well below rating — say 60 °C when the part is rated 90 °C — is a thermostat that is not closing. A curve that climbs normally and then keeps climbing is a flow problem or a stuck-closed valve.

Two: compare three temperatures with an infrared thermometer. Measure at the engine outlet (upper hose, near the thermostat housing), at the radiator inlet, and at the radiator outlet. On a working system the drop across the radiator is real and repeatable. If the engine outlet is hot and the radiator inlet is cold, coolant is not being let through. If both are hot but the radiator outlet is barely cooler than the inlet, the radiator is not shedding heat — which is a radiator problem, not a pump or thermostat problem, and this is the check that catches it before a part gets replaced.

Three: listen and look at the pump itself. With the engine off, check the pump pulley for play and the housing for seepage. Run the engine and listen for bearing noise that tracks engine speed. On a belt-driven pump, a trace of dried coolant at the weep hole is a seal on its way out — the bearing usually follows, because the same coolant that escapes past the seal washes the bearing grease out.

If all three checks point at nothing, stop and pressure-test the system cold. A slow external leak, a failed cap or combustion gas in the coolant will mimic both parts, and no parts cannon will fix any of them.

Thermostat: Open, Closed and Everything Between

The valve has three failure modes, and they are not interchangeable. A wax-element thermostat fails progressively: the element weakens, the opening temperature drifts down, and the valve starts to hang part-open before it sticks outright.

Failure modeTemperature behaviourCabin heatTypical codeCommercial consequence
Stuck openRuns cold; slow warm-up; cools further at highway speedWeak but presentP0128Fuel consumption and emissions rise; drivable for weeks, so the customer postpones
Stuck closedWarms normally, then climbs fast once the valve should openOften still strong, via the bypass circuitUsually noneHead gasket and warped head risk; this is the failure that turns a cheap part into an engine job
Sticking / part-openRepeats a sawtooth: hot, cool, hot on one driveFluctuates with the gaugeSometimes P0128, sometimes nothingHardest to sell because the fault is intermittent; scan logs are the evidence
Wrong rating fittedStable but offset from specificationDepends on the offsetP0128 or noneRepeat comeback after a “successful” repair; check the stamp on the old part

Two details decide whether the repair holds. The first is the rating: fit the number the engine was calibrated for, not the one that happens to be on the shelf. The second is the housing. On a growing share of modern engines — VW and Audi EA111 and EA888 families, several Mercedes-Benz four-cylinders — the thermostat is moulded into a plastic housing with the sensor and seal integrated. Replacing only the insert on those engines means reusing a housing that has already been heat-cycled for a decade, and the leak returns at the seam rather than the valve. Sell the complete housing for those applications.

Water Pump: Seal, Bearing, Impeller

Three failure paths, and only two of them leave evidence outside the pump.

The seal goes first, almost always. The weep hole under the pump snout is a deliberate drain: when the shaft seal starts to pass, coolant escapes there instead of into the bearing or the sump. What a technician finds is not usually a puddle but a chalky trail — the dye and mineral residue left after the water evaporates. On a hot engine that trail is the whole diagnosis.

The bearing follows the seal. Once coolant has washed the grease out, the bearing howls, whines or grinds, and the pulley develops play. A pulley with visible wobble is a stopped-engine situation: a shaft that lets go can throw the belt, take the fan with it and destroy the radiator.

The impeller fails silently. This is the one that produces no leak and no noise. A plastic or pressed-metal impeller can crack, corrode, spin on the shaft or separate from it entirely, and the pump looks perfect from outside while moving almost nothing. The signature is overheating under load with a full system, a heater that weakens as revs rise, and a radiator that never gets properly hot. A pump that has run on the wrong coolant, or on plain water, is the usual candidate.

On an electrically driven pump the whole diagnostic changes. There is no belt, no pulley and no weep hole worth watching. The pump is commanded by the engine management, so the test is a scan-tool activation with the coolant temperature watched live, plus a check of supply voltage and the associated fault memory. Replacing an electric pump because of a corroded connector is an expensive way to learn that lesson.

P0128 Is Not an Overheating Code

P0128 means “coolant temperature below thermostat regulating temperature”: the engine did not warm up as fast as the calibration expects. It is the opposite of an overheating complaint, and reading it as one sends people down the wrong path.

The most common cause by a wide margin is a thermostat stuck open, followed by a coolant temperature sensor reporting low, a low coolant level leaving air at the sensor, and a cooling fan that runs continuously. Note what is absent from that list: the water pump. A pump that is not circulating usually causes overheating, not under-temperature, because the engine keeps its heat instead of losing it.

So P0128 plus a cold-running engine is a thermostat sale. P0128 plus a normal gauge and a sensor reading that disagrees with an infrared thermometer at the hose is a sensor sale. P0128 plus overheating is neither, and the two faults need to be diagnosed separately rather than assumed to share a cause.

Still Overheating After the Thermostat Was Changed

This is the most common comeback in the category, and it has a short list of causes worth working through in order.

Air in the system. The single most frequent cause. Modern cooling systems have bleed points at the heater hose, the thermostat housing or an expansion tank cap, and some require a vacuum fill or a specific warm-up and cool-down cycle. An engine with an air pocket behaves exactly like one with a failing pump: the gauge climbs, the heater goes cold at idle, and the radiator stays cool.

The housing was reused. A new insert in a warped plastic housing leaks at the seam, behind the sensor, or past an O-ring that has gone flat. It looks like the repair failed when in fact only half the part was replaced.

The pump was the fault all along. A stuck-closed thermostat and a dead impeller produce the same symptom, and the thermostat is the cheaper guess. If the temperature still climbs after a correct thermostat and a correct bleed, measure flow before buying another valve.

The radiator, fan or cap. A radiator restricted internally will pass enough coolant to idle happily and fail under load. A fan that never runs turns every traffic jam into an overheat. A cap that will not hold pressure lowers the boiling point and produces steam at normal temperatures.

Combustion gas. A failing head gasket pressurises the system, pushes coolant out of the expansion tank and leaves the loop unable to transfer heat. A chemical block test on the coolant takes ten minutes and settles it.

Replace One, or Both?

The honest answer is that it depends on labour access, not on parts philosophy. Where both components sit behind the same covers — common on transverse four-cylinders and on several V6 layouts — the second part costs a fraction of the first in labour, and replacing it pre-emptively is sound economics. Where the pump is driven off the accessory belt and the thermostat sits in an accessible housing, replacing a healthy part adds cost and a new failure point for no benefit.

Platform familyPump driveThermostat arrangementWhat to replace together
BMW N52 / N54 / N55Electric, ECU-controlledSeparate housing, map-controlledPump, thermostat, coolant; bleed via scan tool
BMW M52 / M54Mechanical, belt-drivenHousing with gasketPump, thermostat, housing gasket, belt if contaminated
Mercedes-Benz M112 / M113Mechanical, belt-drivenSeparate housing, O-ring sealedPump, thermostat, housing O-ring
Mercedes-Benz M270 / M274Mechanical, belt-drivenIntegrated plastic housingComplete housing assembly; pump if mileage is high
VW / Audi EA111, EA888Mechanical, belt or chain drivenIntegrated plastic housing with sensorComplete housing, pump, coolant
Toyota 1GR / 2TRMechanical, belt-drivenSeparate housing with rubber gasketThermostat and gasket; pump on condition

One rule survives every platform: replace the coolant. Old coolant that has lost its inhibitor package is what kills the next pump, and mixing two chemistries — typically an OAT with an older silicate formula — produces the gel that blocks heater cores. Flush, fill with the specified type, and bleed properly. The labour is charged either way.

Buying: References, Housings and What Actually Sells

Three decisions shape a cooling-system order, and each one has a failure mode worth knowing before the container is booked.

Insert or assembly. European applications increasingly want the complete housing because the insert alone is not what fails. Stock the assembly for VW/Audi EA111 and EA888, Mercedes-Benz M270 and M274, and the plastic-housing BMW engines; stock the plain insert for older cast-housing applications where price drives the sale.

Pump construction. Metal impellers outlast plastic ones and cost cents more to make, not dollars. Ask for the impeller material and the seal type on the datasheet — a supplier who cannot name either is buying on price from someone else. For hot-climate markets, specify the higher-temperature seal compound.

Kit completeness. A pump sold with its gasket and O-ring sells to a workshop; a bare pump sells to whoever is prepared to chase a seal separately. The same applies to thermostats: housing, seal and sensor in one box removes a phone call from the job.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I know if it is the thermostat or the water pump?
Start with behaviour rather than parts. An engine that never reaches temperature, or warms up very slowly, points to a thermostat stuck open. An engine that warms normally and then overheats under load, especially with a heater that weakens as revs rise, points to circulation — the pump. A pump that leaks or growls is confirmed by inspection; a thermostat is confirmed by the warm-up curve on a scan tool.

Can I drive with a stuck-open thermostat?
Yes, for a while. It will not overheat the engine; it will run cold, use more fuel, produce more emissions and give weak cabin heat, and it will usually set P0128. Weeks are acceptable, months are not, because an engine running rich for a long period dilutes the oil and loads the catalyst.

Can I drive with a failing water pump?
Only until the temperature gauge moves. Once a pump stops circulating, the head reaches damaging temperatures in minutes, and the difference between a pump replacement and a head gasket job is measured in how long the driver kept going. A noisy or leaking pump with normal temperatures is a repair to schedule immediately, not a reason to stop at the roadside.

Why does my heater blow cold when the engine is hot?
The heater core is the highest point in the loop and the first place to lose flow. Air in the system, a pump with a failing impeller or a partially blocked core all produce the same symptom. If the heater recovers when you raise the revs, suspect flow; if it never recovers, suspect air or a blockage.

Does a water pump failure always leak?
No. Impeller separation happens entirely inside the pump and leaves no external trace. A pump can be dry, quiet and completely ineffective. That is the case where the infrared comparison across the radiator earns its place in the diagnostic routine.

What is the minimum order for wholesale supply?
Fifty pieces per reference. Pumps, thermostats and housings can be mixed within one order, and both families combine well with brake, gasket or suspension lines in a mixed container. Quotations are issued FOB Guangzhou, usually within 48 hours of receiving the OE list.

Send us your OE list. Photograph the number stamped on the old thermostat or the pump housing, send it over WeChat or through the enquiry form, and we will match it against our cooling range, confirm whether that application needs the complete housing, and quote FOB Guangzhou within 48 hours. Mixed containers are welcome.

title: When Is Canton Fair 2026? Full Phase Schedule for Auto Parts Buyers
description: When is Canton Fair 2026? The 140th session runs 15 October – 4 November 2026 across three five-day phases. Full phase schedule table (Phase 1 auto parts Oct 15-19, Phase 2 Oct 23-27, Phase 3 Oct 31-Nov 4), Pazhou complex hall map, daily opening hours 09:30-18:00, the three-day move-in gaps, and a 7-day trip plan for auto parts buyers.

content:
Every October the same five questions land in our in-box from auto parts distributors, importers and brand buyers across Africa, the Gulf, the CIS and Latin America. The first one — "when is Canton Fair 2026?" — is the easiest to answer. The second, third, fourth and fifth ("which phase covers auto parts?", "do I need a buyer badge?", "how long do I need in Guangzhou?", "is it worth combining with a factory visit?") are the ones that decide whether you actually place orders, or just walk the halls for three days and fly home with a tote bag.

This guide is a single, dated reference for the full Canton Fair 2026 schedule — Phase 1, 2 and 3 dates, opening hours, the auto parts halls, the three-day move-in gaps, and how an auto parts buyer should plan a seven-day trip around the calendar. Everything below is cross-checked against the official China Import and Export Fair site (cantonfair.org.cn) and the venue operator's published hall map. Dates are correct as of 8 October 2026. Re-confirm closer to your travel date, as the organizer occasionally adjusts single-day maintenance windows.

01 What "When Is Canton Fair 2026?" Really Means for an Auto Parts Buyer

The headline answer is short. Canton Fair 2026 runs from 15 October to 4 November 2026, broken into three five-day phases with three-day move-out / move-in intervals in between. For the 140th session the organizer has renamed the phases thematically — "Advanced Manufacturing" (Phase 1), "Quality Home Life" (Phase 2) and "Better Life" (Phase 3) — but the underlying hall layout is the same as in previous years.

For an auto parts buyer, the follow-up question is even more important: which of those three weeks contains your category? The answer is firmly Phase 1, 15–19 October 2026. Vehicles, two-wheelers, auto components, auto electronics, motorcycle parts, NEV charging hardware, and the wider "advanced manufacturing" cluster all sit inside Phase 1. Phases 2 and 3 carry home, gift, fashion and lifestyle categories — useful for some buyers who mix product lines, but irrelevant if your business is purely automotive aftermarket or OEM-grade parts.

The other common misreading is to assume the fair is one continuous event. It is not. Each phase has its own exhibitor list, its own hall map, and its own peak visitor days. Most overseas auto parts buyers fly in for Phase 1 only, then either return home or move on to a factory visit in the Pearl River Delta during the 20–22 October break before Phase 1 ends. We will get to that cadence in section 6.

02 The 140th Canton Fair at a Glance: Five Dates You Need to Circle

If you only memorize five lines, memorize these. They are the dates that determine flights, hotel blocks, visa timing, and which week your team is on the ground in Guangzhou.

MarkerDateWhy it matters
Phase 1 opens (auto parts)15 October 2026 (Thursday)Doors open 09:30. First-mover advantage on brake, filter, suspension and electrical suppliers.
Phase 1 closes19 October 2026 (Monday)Last day of the only auto-parts-relevant week. Most overseas buyers depart 19–20 Oct.
Move-in gap (1)20–22 October 2026Three-day hall reset. Use this for a same-province factory visit (Guangdong auto parts belt).
Phase 2 opens23 October 2026 (Friday)Houseware / gifts / building materials. Skip unless you mix categories.
Phase 2 closes27 October 2026 (Tuesday)—
Move-in gap (2)28–30 October 2026Second three-day gap. Final window for new supplier negotiations before Phase 3.
Phase 3 opens31 October 2026 (Saturday)Toys, fashion, home textiles, stationery, health. Not relevant to auto parts.
Phase 3 closes (fair ends)4 November 2026 (Wednesday)Official end of the 140th Canton Fair. Online platform continues year-round.

Auto parts distributors who only have one week of leave will, in almost every case, book around 13–21 October. That gives you Phase 1 in full plus the move-in gap for a same-province factory detour.

03 The Full Phase Schedule: What Runs When, and What Closes When

Here is the full 21-day window in one table, with the daily opening hours, the relevant product clusters, and the typical reason an overseas buyer would attend each phase.

PhaseDates 2026Daily hoursCluster nameWhy an auto parts buyer might attend
Phase 115–19 Oct (Thu–Mon)09:30 – 18:00Advanced ManufacturingCore auto parts week: vehicles, two-wheelers, NEV, auto electronics, hardware, lighting
Move-in20–22 Oct— (halls closed)—Use for same-province factory visit (Guangzhou, Foshan, Dongguan, Huizhou)
Phase 223–27 Oct (Fri–Tue)09:30 – 18:00Quality Home LifeHouseware, gifts, decorations, building materials — only if you mix categories
Move-in28–30 Oct— (halls closed)—Follow-up meetings, price renegotiation, sample consolidation
Phase 331 Oct – 4 Nov (Sat–Wed)09:30 – 18:00Better LifeToys, fashion, stationery, health, pet — not relevant to auto parts

The total on-site window is 15 trading days spread across 21 calendar days. That is a long, slow fair, not a five-day sprint. Plan your trip length to match.

04 Why Phase 1 Is the Only Phase Most Auto Parts Buyers Need

Phase 1 of the 140th Canton Fair is, for the global auto parts industry, the most important single week of the year. It is where the bulk of brake, filter, suspension, electrical, engine, transmission and rubber-moulded part suppliers are physically present under one roof. If you only attend one phase, it is Phase 1.

Three operational reasons reinforce this. First, supplier concentration: by the organizer's published hall plan, the vehicle and component halls sit in Areas A and B of the Pazhou complex, with overflow in the International Pavilion for cross-border sellers. Second, decision-maker presence: factory owners, export managers and tooling engineers typically attend only Phase 1, because that is the week their customers fly in. Third, lead-time alignment: most export orders placed in mid-October can be tooled, sampled, and shipped before the Chinese New Year factory shutdown in late January / early February, which matters for distributors building inventory for Q1 and Q2 of the following year.

Phases 2 and 3 do still see a small number of crossover auto accessories exhibitors (dash cams, interior trim, organizers, lighting upgrades), but the engine of the auto parts business is unambiguously Phase 1.

05 Which Halls Cover Auto Parts: Vehicles, Two Wheels and Advanced Manufacturing

The Pazhou complex is divided into five lettered areas (A, B, C, D, plus the International Pavilion) spread along the Pearl River. For 2026, the organizer has grouped auto parts into the "Advanced Manufacturing" cluster, which physically sits in Areas A and B. The table below maps the main auto-related hall names as referenced in the 140th session hall plan.

Hall cluster (2026 name)What you will find thereTypical buyer goal
Vehicles & Two WheelsComplete vehicles, motorcycles, e-bikes, three-wheelers, NEV passenger cars, light commercial vehiclesDistributor appointments, model comparisons, OEM/ODM discussions
Auto Parts & ComponentsBrake systems, filters, suspension, steering, engine parts, transmission, exhaust, rubber mouldingsAftermarket and OEM-grade sourcing, OE cross-reference
Auto Electronics & AccessoriesSensors, dashboards, lighting, infotainment, TPMS, dashcams, wiring harnessesNew-line product discovery, retrofit opportunities
NEV & ChargingEV components, charging hardware, battery thermal management, electric drive systemsForward-looking sourcing for 2027+ model years
Hardware & ToolsHand tools, power tools, garage equipmentOften bought alongside parts (workshop owners)
International PavilionCross-border e-commerce sellers, trading companies, brand agentsSmaller MOQ transactions, niche brand discovery

Note that hall numbers and exact groupings can shift year-on-year. Always re-confirm with the official venue map 7–10 days before you fly.

06 Three Phases, Three-Plus-Week Window: How the Intervals Affect Your Trip

The biggest planning mistake first-time Canton Fair visitors make is assuming the three phases run back-to-back. They do not. Between Phase 1 closing on 19 October and Phase 2 opening on 23 October, there is a full three-day gap, and the same again between Phase 2 and Phase 3. Those gaps are not optional rest days — they are hard move-out / move-in windows when the halls are physically closed for booth teardown, reconfiguration, and fresh exhibitor load-in.

For an auto parts buyer, those gaps are actually useful. If you are sourcing from Guangzhou or anywhere in the Pearl River Delta — Foshan, Dongguan, Huizhou, Zhongshan, Shenzhen — you can use the 20–22 October break to visit two or three factories in person, then return to Pazhou for a final round of follow-up meetings at the end of Phase 1 (some exhibitors stay late on 19 October for dinners and private meetings). Buyers from further afield often use the gap to fly to Shenzhen for cross-province factory visits, or to consolidate samples in a Guangzhou bonded warehouse.

What you cannot do is walk halls during the gap days. If your travel budget only allows one week, build the calendar around Phase 1 plus a same-province factory day, not around a hypothetical three-week grand tour.

07 The Daily Clock: Opening Hours, Last Entry and Travel Time

The official daily hours for the 140th Canton Fair are 09:30 to 18:00, all three phases, with the final entry cut-off typically around 16:30 to allow visitors time to reach the outer halls before close. Last exit is generally 17:30, with exhibitor-only teardown beginning at 18:00 sharp. Weekend days (17–18 October, 24–25 October, 31 October – 1 November) are full trading days — there is no "weekend only for locals" rule.

In practical terms, an experienced buyer's day at the fair looks like this:

TimeWhat you do
08:00 – 09:00Breakfast at hotel, review the day's booth shortlist, queue at metro
09:15At Pazhou complex gate, badge ready
09:30 – 12:30First wave of booth visits (most senior managers freshest in the morning)
12:30 – 13:30Lunch in the on-site food court or at a nearby hotel buffet
13:30 – 17:00Second wave: back to morning leads, sample pickup, pricing negotiation
17:00 – 18:00Cold-call walk of new halls, hand out business cards, set up next-day meetings
19:00 onwardsIndustry dinners, hosted by exhibitors or local sourcing agents (often the most useful part of the day)

Travel time from central Guangzhou (Tianhe / Yuexiu) to the Pazhou complex is 25–45 minutes by metro Line 8 (Xingang Dong station for Area A, Pazhou station for Area B), or 30–60 minutes by taxi depending on Pazhou bridge traffic. Plan to be at the gate no later than 09:15 if you want a productive first hour.

08 How the 2026 Calendar Compares to Spring 2026 and Autumn 2025

The 140th Canton Fair follows the same spring/autumn cadence that has run since 1957. The Spring 2026 session (the 139th) ran 15 April – 5 May 2026 on the identical three-phase, five-day, three-gap structure. The Autumn 2025 session (the 138th) ran 15 October – 4 November 2025 on the same skeleton. The 140th is, by design, a continuation — same venue, same hours, same exhibitor categories, with only the new "Advanced Manufacturing / Quality Home Life / Better Life" branding changes.

For an auto parts buyer this consistency is operationally useful. Pricing trends you observed in spring 2026 (filter media, brake friction, rubber compounds) will, broadly, hold into autumn 2026 with seasonal adjustments. Container freight rates, raw steel and copper indices, and the RMB/USD corridor are usually the bigger swing factors than the fair's own calendar. The other continuity is online: the Canton Fair online platform runs year-round, so any supplier you met in April 2026 is still reachable in October 2026 through the same buyer login.

The 140th session's specific improvements, per the organizer's own announcements, are better international buyer fast-track lanes at the entrance gates, expanded on-site translation services, and a refreshed International Pavilion layout to accommodate more cross-border e-commerce exhibitors.

09 Coordinating Your Trip: Flights, Hotels and the Guangzhou Transport Grid

Flights into Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport (CAN) are heaviest on the Monday and Friday before each phase opens, which is why smart buyers arrive on Wednesday or Thursday for Phase 1 (15 October) and depart on the Tuesday or Wednesday after (20–21 October). Hotel rates in the Pazhou / Zhujiang New Town corridor typically triple in the 48 hours before Phase 1 opens, so lock rooms 6–8 weeks in advance.

Within the city, the metro is the only sensible way to reach Pazhou at opening time. Line 8 runs directly to Xingang Dong (Area A) and Pazhou (Area B) stations. Allow at least 30 minutes from a Tianhe hotel. Taxis are usable after 18:00 once the metro thins out, but the Pazhou bridge approach can add 20–30 minutes during the morning rush.

For buyers who also want a same-province factory visit during the 20–22 October gap, we typically arrange a half-day Guangzhou warehouse inspection and a one-night stay in Foshan or Dongguan, then a return to Guangzhou for outbound flight on 22 or 23 October. The whole arc — Phase 1 plus a Pearl River Delta factory detour — fits cleanly inside an eight-day window.

10 Frequently Asked Questions

When is Canton Fair 2026 — is it the same week every year?

Yes, the autumn session reliably runs 15 October to 4 November, broken into three five-day phases. The 140th session in 2026 follows the same skeleton, with Phase 1 on 15–19 October, Phase 2 on 23–27 October, and Phase 3 on 31 October – 4 November. Spring sessions run 15 April to 5 May on the identical structure.

Which phase of Canton Fair 2026 covers auto parts?

Phase 1 (15–19 October 2026). The "Advanced Manufacturing" cluster in Areas A and B of the Pazhou complex houses vehicles, two-wheelers, auto parts, auto electronics, NEV components and related hardware. Phases 2 and 3 do not feature auto parts as a primary category.

Do I need a visa to attend Canton Fair 2026?

Overseas buyers typically need a Chinese business visa (M visa) or a tourist visa (L visa) depending on the issuing country's agreement with China. The Canton Fair organizer can issue an official invitation letter to registered overseas buyers, which materially helps the visa appointment. Apply at least 6–8 weeks before travel; some consulates are faster, some slower.

How long should I plan to stay in Guangzhou for the auto parts week?

Most first-time auto parts buyers stay 5–7 days. A typical plan is: arrive Tuesday or Wednesday, attend the full Phase 1 week (15–19 Oct), use the 20–22 October gap for a same-province factory visit, and depart Friday or Saturday. Buyers who also want a deeper factory audit often extend to 10–12 days.

Can I attend Canton Fair without a buyer badge?

No. All overseas visitors must hold a Canton Fair buyer badge, obtained through the official pre-registration portal. The badge is free but takes 3–7 working days to process after identity verification. On-site registration is technically possible but the queues on Phase 1 opening day are long enough to cost you a productive morning.

Is the Canton Fair still worth attending in the age of online sourcing?

Yes, for the auto parts category specifically. The physical fair concentrates 5,000+ component exhibitors in one venue for five trading days, with decision-makers present and sample stocks on hand. Online platforms are excellent for follow-up and small re-orders, but they cannot replicate a 20-minute booth-side negotiation with the factory owner standing next to you. The two channels are complementary, not competing.

Where is Globalucar during Canton Fair 2026?

Our Guangzhou office is open year-round at approximately 30 minutes' drive from the Pazhou complex. During fair season we offer in-person meetings at our office, accompanied factory visits to verified OEM-grade partners in the Pearl River Delta, and live sample comparison against your existing OE references. Reach out to our team ahead of your trip to lock a slot — calendar fills quickly in the 10 days before Phase 1 opens.

title: Ford Engine Oil Cooler OE Number Buyer’s Guide
description: Compare Ford engine oil cooler OE references, verify fitment and identification, and prepare RFQs with clear MOQ, quotation, and receiving checks.
content:
What This Guide Covers

This guide provides a practical framework for buyers searching for a Ford engine oil cooler wholesale source. It brings the listed Ford engine oil cooler OE numbers into one cross-reference table so procurement teams can compare identifiers before requesting a quotation. The identifiers include BB3Q-6B624-EA, H6BG-6B856-DA, HX7G-6B856-AA, 1S7E-6A642-CC, 3C3Z-6A642-CA, 3C3Z-6A642-CA/R, 6790424780, 7S7G-6B856A4A, /1925463, /1778546, 8C3Z-6A642-A, AG9G6S642BC, /LR025515, and //J7BG-7J389-AB.

Every listed item is identified in the catalogue as an Engine Oil Cooler, and the stated vehicle application is Ford. One entry also lists RANGE in its fitment data. The guide avoids unsupported vehicle, engine, port, or dimensional claims and focuses on verified identifiers, catalogue product pages, material, commercial terms, and receiving checks. Each linked product is listed as aluminium, with MOQ 10 pieces, a 12-month warranty, and supply by RFQ.

A consolidated identification table is particularly useful for importers and distributors managing several references. However, the product description and OE marking on an incoming unit should still be checked against the purchase order. Exact character handling is essential because related identifiers can differ only by a prefix, suffix, or slash.

How to Identify the Right Part

Start with the OE number recorded for the required engine oil cooler. Search the table in this guide, then open the corresponding product page to confirm the exact part name and OE reference. Keep punctuation and every segment unchanged when recording the identifier for purchasing or inventory purposes.

Pay particular attention to related references. The catalogue groups 7S7G-6B856A4A, /1925463, and /1778546 under one product. It also records AG9G6S642BC and /LR025515 together. A related-reference group is a search aid, not permission to change the identifier printed on the required part. Confirm the full number, including suffixes such as -EA, -CC, or /R, before issuing a purchase order.

The pictured Ford H6BG-6B856-DA engine oil cooler should be identified by the H6BG-6B856-DA marking rather than by visual similarity alone. The same inspection discipline applies to the Ford 3C3Z-6A642-CA/R engine oil cooler, where retaining the /R suffix is essential for accurate identification.

For physical inspection, compare the complete OE marking on the part with the required reference, check the aluminium material stated for the catalogue product, and inspect the unit and its connections for shipping damage. Because no detailed dimensions, connection layouts, or engine applications are supplied in the facts for this guide, those characteristics should not be inferred from appearance alone.

Importers should avoid replacing a verified reference with a shorter or normalized form. For example, a leading slash, a double slash, and a suffix can be meaningful catalogue characters. The same string used in the RFQ, purchase order, carton label, ERP record, and receiving report supports traceability from enquiry through inspection.

OE Number Cross-Reference

The following table reproduces every OE number from the catalogue facts. It is designed for initial identification only. A matching number is the starting point for an RFQ; final confirmation should also use the complete part description and the marking on the goods received.

OE NumberPart Name
BB3Q-6B624-EAEngine Oil Cooler BB3Q-6B624-EA for Ford / RANGE
/1778546Engine Oil Cooler 7S7G-6B856A4A / /1925463 for Ford

1S7E-6A642-CCEngine Oil Cooler 1S7E-6A642-CC for Ford
